title: A Review of the 2026 Games Workshop Grand Narrative
content:
This past weekend more than 350 players - most from the United States - converged on the Hyatt Regency in downtown Atlanta for the fifth annual Games Workshop Grand Narrative. The Grand Narrative is, for all intents and purposes, the narrative event for the game, and is the only such event which can boast an actual canon story for its characters and players.

In this review, we'll be covering not just this year's Grand Narrative but the event itself, with everything you need to know about its format and how it works. If you've ever wondered what it's like to be at the event and what goes down, this is your inside scoop.

The Format

Players at the Grand Narrative are split into three faction groups before the event begins based on the faction they're playing - Imperium, Chaos, and Interlopers, the catchall group for the game's Xenos factions. These represent the larger narrative forces arrayed around whatever planet/system is being besieged over the following three days.

From there players play six total games as part of their regularly scheduled program, two per day, broken up between briefings, with a morning, midday, and evening briefing to bookend the games. It's during these briefings that the campaign's warlords make their appearances to the assembled player crowd, talking about their backstories and making their agendas known. These set the scene for players in the coming game, letting them know how things are going and giving them hints about what to do next.

At the end there's a final presentation to show off the aftermath of the narrative, letting players know how their actions influenced the story, along with awards given out for everything from best costume to who was the campaign's biggest dickhead (the antagonist), narratively speaking. The whole event has a loose, laid-back atmosphere, with games being given time to breathe and players given extra time to hang out and chat between games.

Players coordinate during this on a Discord run by us here at Tabletop Battles, where they can talk amongst themselves both in- and out-of-character, show off their armies and cosplay, and receive announcements, room assignments, and campaign information during the event.

Skari as Arathiel, the Ninth Sail

The Warlords

The stars of the Grand Narrative are the warlords, Games Workshop staff who take on the roles of the campaign's key main characters. When you play the Grand Narrative, it's not so much your story as it is theirs - the story isn't so much about your Warlord and their army but rather those Warlords. And your games and actions are more about how you influence those Warlords and their story. Certain players may have an outsized influence on those stories through their actions, but generally the idea is that it's their story, and you're here to help tell it.

The 2026 Grand Narrative featured five Warlords (usually there are six):

  • Kaelen Voss, the Free Captain - The Space Marine at the heart of the whole thing. A former Executioner who left to join Huron's rebellion, then got sick of Huron when he realized the Tyrant of Badab was just another Tyrant. Voss fled and conquered the planet of Ferrum's Wake, liberating it and advocating freedom at all costs. Voss is kind of obviously doomed and delusional - no one is free in the 41st millennium - in a way that's vaguely endearing if you pretend not to know how the galaxy works. He's a Chaos Space Marine who doesn't worship Chaos, which also puts him in a weird spot - he ostensibly appeals more to renegade or rebellious Imperial players and factions than Chaos followers, but there are plenty of players out there who like Chaos but don't actually want to admit to worshipping the evil gods of Space Hell.
  • The Warrant - A mysterious daemonic (?) entity tracking down Voss on behalf of Huron Blackheart. The Warrant is the "loyal to Chaos" side of the Chaos faction, carries an axe, yells about the pantheon a lot, and is mostly here with the straightforward goal of claiming skulls and killing Voss. He's kind of a weird loser beneath Huron's notice and hoping to claim fame and glory by killing Voss. It's unclear if this will actually work.
  • Commander Orestes Morn - A gruff, no-nonsense Imperial Commander who believes in discipline above all else. You know the kind - cold, hard, imperious, and dead set on punishing treachery with the fires of his void ships, letting the Emperor sort out the souls of the faithful. The kind of typical hardass you see in these things who won't listen to reason and shows off how inflexible the religious zealotry of the Imperium can be.
  • Mara Venn, Reluctant Saint - A commoner among the free people of Ferrum's Wake, Venn is a guerilla fighter trying desperately to save her people from Voss' inflicted cruelty and the Imperial bombardments. She focuses on saving her frightened people while raiding armories, rigging bombs, and moving through the shadows. A few close calls and weird coincidences have people calling her a saint.
  • Arathiel, the Ninth Sail - A bold and arrogant Anrathe captain, leading a force of plunderers, marauders, and raiders across the face of Ferrum's Wake for some unknown goal. They seem focused primarily on plunder and having a good time clashing with Imperial and Chaos forces alike. Arathiel is the kind of comedic, scenery-chewing scoundrel that does best at these kinds of things, able to be bombastic and over the top without being so self-serious that the performance collapses under its own attempted weight.

The lack of a sixth warlord option for the Xenos here was unfortunate, as not giving them a second option felt a bit lame, particularly given the associated rules for each warlord.

The Brave Soldiers of Imperial Battlegroup 5

The Battlegroups

Before the event, players are organized into groups of of roughly ten players each called Battlegroups. These are the players you'll be campaigning with over the course of the campaign, loosely aligned to the same goals and making some decisions as a group. Each round, your battlegroup is paired into another rival battlegroup, and with rare exception, always against a battlegroup of a rival faction team, i.e. you don't tend to see Imperium vs. Imperium infighting unless a special game declares it or a player really wants to pretend to be a turncoat. Each battlegroup also had one or two Kill Team players, who represented the special forces/operations part of that team.

How much you interact with your battlegroup is up to you. In my experience, this format works best when you have friends in your group, as you'll be in the same rooms playing with those people over the course of your six games and it makes coordinating group activities easier. If you're not in a battlegroup with people you know, it's a bit more of a mixed bag - I've met some really great people in prior years this way, and I've also had years where I just didn't talk to any of them. That's partly because while a lot of the Tabletop Battles crew show up to the Grand Narrative, most of them play as Imperium factions, meaning we generally aren't allowed to be on the same team.

This is a rough quirk of the team/battlegroup system - You are more or less forced into a faction choice based on your campaign alignment. While this largely makes sense - you do want most of your chaos forces to be chaos forces - it also has a few odd consequences, like making it so you are very likely to end up only playing against space marines for the entire event if you're not on team Imperium. It also means the campaign results end up skewed a bit by how good a Codex or set of Codexes are - it's no coincidence that Xenos have historically done well when the Eldar books were strongest, and this year's Imperial result has a lot to do with Space Marines being overtuned. Winning or losing your games doesn't necessarily affect the story, but being able to do your narrative goal is a hell of a lot easier if you beat the brakes off your opponent.

For this year's campaign, each battlegroup was called to pledge their loyalty to a warlord before the campaign began (with Xenos groups having the option to serve a nebulous "voidborne horrors" instead of Arathiel, if they so chose). My battlegroup took a vote and narrowly chose to support the Warrant, at least initially. Not one battlegroup aligned to Voss in this initial offering, but late in the campaign players were allowed to secretly change their allegiance, at which point around 30ish players did, including about half of my battlegroup. I was literally running Red Corsairs, so defecting to a guy who betrayed Huron was never going to happen.

Once you pledge yourself to your warlord of choice, each player in your group is given an Ascendancy card, which has benefits (buffs) and consequences (debuffs) for your army depending on how well your faction is doing in the campaign. These were wildly unbalanced, ranging from game-breaking to fairly mid, and the Chaos ones in particular had some heinous drawbacks - Voss' let your units advance/fall back and perform an action at the lowest levels and still shoot/charge at the highest levels, but you'd take leadership debuffs at every level. Trying to make Dark Pacts on a 9+ across my army sounds like a nightmare and being able to advance and do an action is meaningless when you spend the whole game battle-shocked.

The Briefings

Before the event, and between every round of games, players are called down to a shared space for a Briefing. These briefings see each Lord of War come out and talk about how things are going, advancing the plot, dispensing new information about how things are going, and then giving players an idea of what they need to do in the next round. These are bookended by a quick reading to set the stage and a note at the end about which level of ascendancy your faction is currently in.

These play out with a lot of bluster, and resemble dinner theater more than anything else. They're a lot of fun, and work best when the actors themselves aren't trying to be too serious. They're often limited by what they can do within the confines of the space and the costumes, and this can be a challenge when they want characters to meaningfully interact in a scene. One particularly rough spot this year had the Warrant come face to face with Voss after the first round, and neither of them fight, which seems very strange given the Warrant's stated goal of killing Voss. I'd later learn that this wasn't intended to be a face-to-face conversation, but it didn't end up coming across that way at all and so it just looked like the two characters were posturing at each other instead of fighting.

This year's standouts were Mara Venn (Lydia Grant) and Arathiel (Skari). Lydia always puts on a strong performance at these things and did a particularly fine job this year as the reluctant saint, who would turn out to not be who she claimed. Or who others claimed she was, anyways. Meanwhile Skari's Arathiel was loud, arrogant, and just the right amount of funny for the role, making him a clear fan favorite. Nick Bayton did admirable work as Kaelen Voss, wearing a massive suit of power armor that clearly limited his mobility but looked amazing, though the role of Voss felt less fleshed out than it needed to be. Voss was always clearly going to turn out to be a tyrant in his own right, but it felt like he should have started closer to that endpoint - as a very clear false hope of freedom under a new populist tyrant rather than someone who seems earnest and becomes corrupted later.

Battlegroups square off

The Games

You play six games as a participant in the Grand Narrative, two per day. Each round gives you about four hours to play, and for that round your Battlegroup will be assigned to a room that represents a specific warzone for the campaign. These are typically decorated to resemble that warzone, with extra foliage or scents, and the tables themselves will be themed to match the vibes of that warzone's battlefields.

This year's battlefields in particular were a massive step up from prior years, in that they featured honest-to-god 11th edition terrain footprints, meaning that each table had actual line-of-sight blocking terrain pieces using abstracted lines of sight. The terrain itself was fine as always, a mix of detailed custom terrain, modern prepainted stuff, and the painted ruins and terrain from recent Narrative/competitive events.

The 2026 Narrative tables, now featuring terrain footprints!

You'll notice these aren't standard layouts - they're set up on the table before you get there, and may not be symmetrical. They also don't always work for every deployment, so you kind of have to figure out which deployment map to use when you arrive so that you'll have an adequate number of objectives outside each player's Deployment Zone. Though I heard several players just show up and say "do you want to just do Dawn of War?" without thinking about this. I think that's a natural inclination, especially for people who don't play often, so I'd suggest to GW that they look at taking this into account when setting up layouts in the future.

The missions themselves were... just normal primary missions for 11th edition 40k, based on your Disposition. Before the campaign we were told to pick two Dispositions which matched our Warlord's temperament, then we could only use those during the campaign, even if we swapped armies. This could have been better worded, as I think many players interpreted it to mean they could take those dispositions regardless of what their Detachments allowed.

Pairings are handled via a Tarot Card system, something they introduced a few years ago. At registration you're given a single Imperial Tarot Card and told to keep it for the entire campaign. When you go to your assigned battlefield rooms, you'll head to the table with the matching card, where your corresponding opponent from the opposing battlegroup with the same card will also go. This works fine, but the cards themselves are difficult to read and there's no mind being paid to player skill, faction, or any other factors when using these cards. It's all random - which again, is fine but I really think the event could benefit from some kind of record matching.

A number of the Vox Localum, flanked by The Warrant on the right

Each room is attended by a member or two of the Vox Localum, GW reps acting in roles as servants to the Warlords. Each Warlord had three associated Vox Localum. These reps are responsible for coordinating players when they enter the battlefield rooms, collecting results, and answering questions. They had more to do this year, and were given more chances to interact with the story and send players on quests. One new quirk this year were the custom secondary missions.

That's the other big quirk this year - upon pledging your loyalty to a warlord, you received a special Secondary mission to go in the deck provided to each player at the outset of the event. Every member of the Vox Localum had their own special secondary mission, and you could secure one of these to add/swap into your deck if you interacted with them the right way. This was my favorite addition this year, as it created a great collectible element for players to find while not adding too much cognitive load - you don't have to think about these all the time, you can just put them in your deck, then when you draw them you do what they say, score them, and you're done.

The downside is you can put these in your deck and never see them, especially if you only get one or two. And I think they were a little too hard to get ahold of during the campaign, though I did see players showing off a full set, which was cool.

During the aforementioned briefings you're given a faction goal in addition to the game's primary objective. This will often be vague - something like "collect skulls," "raise the beacons," or "erect shrines to the dark gods." It's largely on you as a player to figure out what this means, and when you report results to the Vox Localum, they'll ask if you won your game and if you accomplished this objective. You honestly kind of make these up - I decided that erecting Chaos Shrines meant doing Cleanse on central objectives, so I went with that. In one round we decided that while I claimed plenty of skulls, I'd thrown them all onto a pyre in the middle of the battlefield, inadvertently creating a beacon like my opponent wanted to create all along (he spent time charging the middle of the table to no avail). If I'm honest, I'd like these to be better defined. I like that you can take some freedom with them, but they often end up feeling either like you're just making up whatever reason you want for them to be a success or you're left wondering what the hell you're supposed to do.

The Story

The story itself was fairly solid this year. Generally speaking, nothing is decided before the event - there are some rough outlines of how things can go and some clear possible endpoints, but the staff meet up between each round to talk about what happened, review results, and figure out what happens next. It's very much organic in that respect, though there are obvious paths planned for some - Mara Venn explored alliances with both the Imperium Commander Morn and Kaelen Voss, and end the end wound up in the Imperial fold. This was the result of player choices and decisions, and she could have gone either way before her final conclusion. More on that in a moment.

Voss talked a big game about freedom and then ended up turning to the Dark Gods for help. Not a big shocker, and he killed the Warrant, who turned out to be a former serf of his desperate for glory and recognition from Huron but was never more than an eager aspirant. Neither was particularly impressive and Voss' new devotion to the dark gods was short-lived, as he was almost immediately shot in the face by Arathiel, who was there to retrieve a soul stone from a fallen former lover/leader from Voss' armor. The entire set of raiding operations had been a ruse, a ploy to draw attention so he could get close to Voss and reclaim his prize. This sounds cooler than it looked in practice - they really needed to have Arathiel stab Voss, not pretend to shoot him - but the concept was solid.

Morn emerged triumphant, and was reconsidering his faith after witnessing and bringing in Mara Venn and her faithful survivors, who were now en route to Terra on an Imperial ship. Of course, this is when we got the big reveal: Venn was a Genestealer Cultist all along, and her faithful a bunch of infected third-generation devotees.

This was probably the coolest aspect of the event, because Imperial players, led by a Custodes player in battlegroup 6 - fought very hard to convince Morn to listen to Venn and take her in. In doing so, they became responsible for the ship full of genestealer cultists headed for Terra. I got an extra chuckle out of this when I spoke to a fellow player named Jason at the baggage carousel in Houston after the event, and he mentioned that when he read her lore initially it read "exactly like the entry for the Reductress Saboteur." Said Custodes player was very unhappy to discover he'd unwittingly betrayed the Imperium, but I think it was a great moment to showcase how players can affect the narrative. Venn could have ended up siding with Voss or neither, or even not getting off the world. There were a number of very interesting ways that could have gone, and the reveal at the end was very well told. A number of players had a feeling she wasn't who she professed to be at the start, but few if any figured out she was a Genestealer in advance.

This was by far the strongest aspect of the event's story. The rest was more generic but told well enough. This year's Vox Localum had a lot more to do and that made a huge difference. They had clear agendas, changed loyalties, and were more interactive with players, making for a much more fun time.

The Setting

Ferrum's Wake was... a planet. We got one paragraph on it being a Forge World and there was one notable location - Emancipation Spaceport - but otherwise we were told much less about it this year. There was no map and even less visual flair and fewer descriptions than when players were fighting in the webway last year. That's a huge miss, as it kept the location from feeling real or substantial, even as it was about to be dragged into the warp. I think they still struggle in this regard, making the location and setting feel real and tying it concretely to the battlefields they're putting out.

Final Thoughts

This year's Grand Narrative was the strongest yet. Not in every aspect - the lack of custom primary missions was a big miss and some of the faction mechanics were a bit too wild - but many of the added elements were a welcome improvement and the games themselves played better on battlefields with actual terrain footprints. The key sticking point of the Grand Narrative continues to be a disconnect between the time and care put into the narrative and costumes versus the game you play on the table and how you interact with it all but many things improved this year and I'm hopeful they'll continue to learn the right lessons and make next year's event even better.

If you've never attended the Grand Narrative, it's worth giving it a shot - there's no one else able to run an event like this at the scale Games Workshop does right now and while some smaller events may be tighter or have more focus, there's something about having 300-plus costumed fans in a room, all invested in the outcome of a narrative campaign. It's one of the most fun events of the year, and the only one on which I regularly bring along my wife and son, because they're liable to have just as much fun as I do.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. title: The 16 rarest and most expensive MTG cards in the world
content:
What are the most expensive MTG cards of all time? Buying singles can be a cheap way to expand your collection, but properly rare Magic: The Gathering cards are a different story, with MTG prices ranging from a few thousand to three million dollars. We don't recommend paying tens of thousands of dollars for a small cardboard rectangle, but it's fun to dream about owning them and goggle at the prices. So we track the most valuable Magic cards and their sale values here.

Much like the world's most expensive Pokémon cards, most expensive Yugioh cards - and, these days, the most expensive Lorcana cards in the Disney TCG - some Magic: The Gathering cards have become ultra-valuable, prized items, ballooning in price on the secondary market.

Generally, it's not simply because they're the best MTG cards. Though the Power 9 do rank among the most valuable Magic cards, many expensive cards come from the oldest MTG sets, and are prized as much for their age and scarcity as their actual effect. Here you'll find a list of the most costly rare Magic cards ever made, along with the highest prices they have sold for.

The 16 most expensive Magic: The Gathering cards are:

  • Pristine Alpha Black Lotus - $3 million
  • The 1/1 One Ring - $2 million
  • Black Lotus Autographed Alpha - $800,000
  • Mox Opal - $108,000
  • Lord of the Pit Alpha - $105,000
  • Timetwister Alpha - $84,000
  • Splendid Genesis - $72,000
  • Vesuvan Doppelganger - $63,000
  • 01/77 Golden Chocobo - $50,000
  • Ancestral Recall Alpha - $36,000
  • Phoenix Heart - $27,500
  • Autographed Captain Jean-Luc Picard - $26,000
  • Euroakus - $25,200
  • Gleaming Gold Smaug - $24,000
  • Time Walk Gamma - $26,400
  • Fraternal Exaltation - $23,750
  • Mox Emerald Alpha - $18,000
  • Underground Sea Alpha - $17,500
  • Mox Sapphire Unlimited- $16,800

Pristine Alpha Black Lotus

Price: $3 million

With the printing of the One of One Ring in 2023, there was a brief window when the Black Lotus wasn't the most valuable magic card of all time. That didn't last long, because in April 2024, Adam Cai of Pristine Collectibles sold a CGC Pristine 10 graded copy of the Alpha Black Lotus for $3 million to an undisclosed private buyer.

Black Lotus is the most powerful card from Magic's original set, and arguably still the most powerful card in the game. MTG's original 'Alpha' printing in 1993 was a particularly short run, so very few copies of Black Lotus even exist. It also has a spot on the MTG Reserved List - a selection of cards that Wizards has sworn never to reprint, keeping their price high on the secondary market.

Besides its mythos, the card is prized for its powerful effect. An artifact that requires no mana to play, Black Lotus adds three mana of any color to your pool, letting you cast powerful spells rapidly in the early game.

Anyone who opened a Lotus in 1993 had no idea that it would be a collectible, so cards weren't treated kindly, which makes this Pristine 10 copy particularly remarkable. While we don't know the origin of this specific card, it's possible it was recently opened by a daring collector cracking product that had remained sealed for over thirty years.

The 1/1 One Ring

Price: $2 million

Printed for the 2023 Lord of the Rings: Tales of Middle-earth set, the 1/1 The One Ring is both the newest and the most expensive magic card on this list. This very special version of the regular The One Ring card replaces the rules text with the ring's elvish inscription.

It also comes with unique art and a gold serial number - 001 / 001. That's right. Only one copy of this card was ever printed.

One of the only cards on this list that was actually designed to be expensive, the hunt for the one-of-one One Ring was heavily marketed, and its prestige drove fans from around the world to open Lord of the Rings packs, praying they would be the lucky ones to find the elusive artifact. A bidding war began before the card was even discovered, and had escalated all the way up to $2 million (plus a paella) before it was eventually found.

Rapper and Magic: the Gathering superfan Post Malone purchased the One Ring card. The lucky chap who found the card, one Brook Trafton, confirmed that he paid a total of $2 million for the blingy piece.

Black Lotus Autographed Alpha

Price: $800,000

Magic: The Gathering's most famous flower is also its most prized card. Long coveted as a collector's piece, a mint-condition Black Lotus from the game's 1993 Alpha set (the first print run of MTG's original core set), signed by illustrator Christopher Rush, sold for a whopping $511,100 / £360,427 in an eBay auction in January 2021.

That would make this Black Lotus the second most expensive MTG card ever sold - except that Post Malone recently claimed to have bought a similar Black Lotus for $800,000. That man really has the monopoly on pricey Magic cards.

Mox Opal

Price: $108,000

Plenty of cards from Magic's Alpha set are worth money in pristine condition, and Mox Opal is no different. It's an esteemed member of the 'Power 9', nine cards from MTG's early sets that are still considered some of the most powerful in the game.

Mox Opal is one of five 'Moxes' found among the Power 9. Each of these offers a very simple effect: add one mana of a particular color to your mana pool. It doesn't sound explosive, but it gives you a way to bypass the standard restriction on how many lands you can play per turn. More mana means bringing stronger cards out faster, and that makes victory far more likely.

Unsurprisingly, Mox Opal and its siblings are banned in most formats. Their power and scarcity, however, mean they're gems of great value. The priciest sale we've seen recently is this PSA 10 copy, which sold for a shiny $108,000.

Lord of the Pit Alpha

Price: $105,000

Lord of the Pit is MTG's original giant black daemon, printed in the game's first set, Alpha. His basic stats would be just about playable in a modern draft as a game ender, as he's a seven / seven with flying and trample that costs seven mana. But creatures in Alpha were dreadful, so this beat stick comes with a very big downside: during your upkeep, you need to sacrifice a creature, or the Lord of the Pit will deal seven damage to you.

He was literally the biggest, scariest creature in the game in 1993, and with both Animate Dead and Dark Ritual in the first set, he could hit the battlefield well before turn seven, so he was a very in-demand card. Since no-one knew Magic was going to be a collectible, the (estimated) 1,008 copies of Lord of the Pit from Alpha saw truly brutal play. A copy of the card, graded Pristine 10 by ratings agency Beckett, sold for $105,000 on auction site Fanatics Collect in 2022.

Timetwister Alpha

Price: $84,000

Timetwister is one of the coveted 'Power 9' cards printed in Alpha, Beta, and Unlimited. These early cards remain staples of most banlists thanks to their explosive abilities, and Timetwister is no exception. Its particular party trick was being the ultimate reset card.

When played, you'll combine your hand, library, and graveyard, give the deck a good shuffle, and draw a fresh seven-card hand. Then, your opponent gets to do the same. It was absurdly good with other fast mana spells, letting you empty your whole hand, and then get a brand-new one.

Found on the Reserved List, Timetwister's price has gradually increased over the years, with the most expensive copy we found evidence of selling on Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC) for an astounding $84,000. 

Splendid Genesis

Price: $72,000

In 1997, Magic founder Richard Garfield wanted to commemorate the creation of something even bigger than a trading card game: a brand-new person. Splendid Genesis is a card that marks the birth of Garfield's first child, and only 110 copies were ever printed.

These cards were never made publicly available. However, Garfield did hand some out to close loved ones, such as Wizards of the Coast employees, family, and friends.

Despite their private distribution, some of these prestigious cards eventually reached the secondary market. The highest-selling copy we found was graded a Near Mint 8 by Beckett, which sold in 2022 for $72,000.

Vesuvan Doppelganger

Price: $63,000

A pretty straightforward case of a Reserved List Alpha card that can't be reprinted, blowing up in value. A good condition copy of this card, graded 9.5 by Beckett, apparently went for a whopping $63,000.

It's a pretty cool clone creature spell that lets you keep swapping the target you're cloning.

01/77 Golden Chocobo

Price: $50,000

This is one of the most recent cards on our list. Wizards of the Coast did its research for the 2025 Final Fantasy set, and realized fans of this franchise are no stranger to dropping absurd amounts of dosh on unlikely collectibles. Then they made them an artifact worth splurging on - one of the first 'headliner' cards.

The serialized Golden Chocobos were the most highly sought card of this record-smashing set, and as there are only 77 of them in existence, they're more valuable than past serialized cards that were in more bountiful supply.

It's hard to know how much of the price tag here comes from their relative rarity, and how much is purely what you might call 'the Final Fantasy factor', but either way, number 1 on the list has been found and sold for a massive $50,000

Ancestral Recall Alpha

Price: $36,000

Ancestral Recall was printed in Alpha and is part of a cycle of cards that gave you three of something for a single colored mana. It shows how little the designers understood the game they had created that this card - which lets you draw three cards for one mana - was assumed to be roughly as powerful as Giant Growth, Lightning Bolt, Dark Ritual, or (of all things) Healing Salve.

Restricted in Vintage and banned in Legacy, Ancestrall Recall is on the Reserved List and is considered part of the Power 9. The highest sale price we've seen is for a Gem Mint 9.5 graded copy, which sold via Heritage Auctions in March 2022 for $36,000 - and $20,000 is a very normal price for a copy of the card in a more ordinary state.

Phoenix Heart

Price: $27,500

Splendid Genesis was one of several cards that MTG creator Richard Garfield used to celebrate life events. In 2014, he designed Phoenix Heart to honor his upcoming wedding to Koni Kim. The number of cards printed is unknown, but we do know that Garfield sent out copies along with his wedding invitations - cute.

In April 2023, a copy of this romantic gesture was sold via Heritage Auctions for $27,500. This grade-8 card was apparently the first time that a copy was available as part of a public auction. Wherever the remaining copies are hiding, they're likely worth even more money if they're in a more pristine condition.

Euroakus

Price: $25,200

Every year, MTG publisher Wizards of the Coast shares Heroes of the Realm cards with its high-performing teams. These cards are printed in extremely limited quantities, and they're unique to the person gifted them - to the point of including the individual recipient's name.

Euroakus was a Heroes of the Realm card given to Wizards' European Team in 2020 for its work promoting MTG and D&D across the continent. The most expensive sale we've seen was when Euroakus went for $25,200 in December 2022. The name has been blurred out in the sale images, so it's not clear who the original owner was.

As you'd expect for one-off cards, Heroes of the Realm pieces are illegal in all formats, with the special exception of Commander. A member of the former Commander rules committee dubbed them legal, but only for the person whose name is on the card - meaning that, as soon as they're sold, they go from functional playing pieces to pure collector's items.

Gleaming Gold Smaug

Price: $24,000

The headliner from The Hobbit set which - off the back of Lord of the Rings' popularity, we might presume - already appears primed to go down in history. With a beautiful golden foil treatment and classic-style art commissioned by Tolkien illustrator Ted Nasmith. Like other recent headliners, only 500 copies exist.

Though we're writing this up before the set has even technically been released, a copy of this card has already sold for $24,000 on eBay. Who can say whether they'll go up or down from here though!

Time Walk Gamma

Price: $26,400

Printed in Alpha and another member of the ultra-rare and ultra-powerful Power 9, Time Walk is a straightforward rulebreaker that lets you take an extra turn for two mana - easy to see why it's on just about every MTG banlist, and restricted to a single copy in Legacy. If you can find a way to recast it from your graveyard, say with a Mystic Sanctuary, you can stop your opponent from ever taking a turn.

This Gamma edition copy is even rarer - it predates Alpha, and is one of the prototype cards used to playtest the game. The 2U mana cost is actually the same as the one blue one generic cost on the printed card - this is just how costs were formatted in Gamma. Interesting to see the additional cost of sacrificing an an island - what on earth happened in playtesting that people thought that cost was too high?

The Gamma edition copy sold via Heritage Auctions for $26,400 in July 2021. The biggest sale for a regular copy of the card is a 9.5 Gem Mint copy, which went for $25,000 in mid-2024 via Heritage Auctions.

Autographed Captain Jean-Luc Picard

Price: $26,00

The 'headliner' cards for the Star Trek set had a little something special extra. Seven textless cards featured hand-written signatures from real Star Trek actors, from William Shatner of TOS to Ethan Peck of Discovery and Strange New Worlds. We don't know how many of each card there are, as they're not numbered, but there's apparently fewer than 250 of each.

After news of Patrick Stewart's sad death, it only made sense that his signed Picard cards would be selling for a little more, and on November 17, one went on eBay for $26,000. Unfortunately, it's possible this one might actually be an overestimate - we can't be sure the seller didn't accept a buyer's best offer instead. However, this price isn't settled yet. It's likely the autographed cards are going to see significant movement in the coming months. 

Fraternal Exaltation

Price: $23,750

When Richard Garfield's second child was born, he created yet another Magic card to commemorate the milestone. Fraternal Exaltation was illustrated by Garfield's sister, Susan, and only around 220 copies were ever made.

As you'd expect, there aren't many Fraternal Exaltations floating around now. A version sold for $23,750 on Heritage Auctions in 2023. This had a CGC grading of only a 6, so if a higher-quality version ever came on the market, we'd expect it to go for a lot more.

Mox Emerald Alpha

Price: $18,000

The five original "Mox" gems were printed in Alpha, Beta, and Unlimited, and are emblematic of how little the team at Wizards of the Coast understood how their game actually worked. Each of these snazzy pieces of jewelry functions similarly to Lands, adding one mana of a single color to your pool at no cost - but while you can only play one Land per turn, you can slap down as many Moxes as you like.

A mox start lets you build up a surge of mana and unleash powerful spells before your opponent has the option of mounting a defense - not counting all the other snazzy things you can trigger by casting an artifact. They're now banned in every format except Vintage, where they're Restricted to a single copy per deck.

Firmly planted in the reserve list, all of the original Moxen are valuable. The Mox Emerald above , from the Alpha printing, sold for $18,000 / £12,700 via Heritage auctions in 2021. You might think folks would prefer to buy a real gemstone with that money.

Underground Sea Alpha

Price: $17,500

A Dual Land that pairs black and blue mana, Underground Sea lets you tap for either color at no additional cost. Although it's just an improved basic Land card, this Alpha set card is particularly prized for having no downside - why use a Land that offers one color, when you could use a Land that offers two?

The most impressive sale we've found coming via Heritage Auctions on 11 April 2024 for $17,500. That was for a gem mint 9.5 copy - as of November 2025, the typical asking price for an Alpha copy was closer to $10k, and Revised printings go for more like $1k.  

Mox Sapphire Unlimited

Price: $16,800

Another of the coveted Mox stones, the Mox Sapphire has the advantage of producing blue mana, the color that gets the most synergy from artifacts. This Mint 10 condition copy from the Unlimited print run sold via Heritage Auctions for $16,800 on May 16, 2019.

If you're interested in the history of magic cards, or know of an amazing high-ticket sale that we haven't added to this guide, we'd love to hear from you in the official Wargamer community! To stay up to date with all of our biggest stories every week, sign up to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: Top 50+ most expensive rare Pokémon cards of all time
content:
What are the most expensive Pokemon cards in the world? After 30 years of regular Pokémon TCG releases, there are quite a few staggeringly valuable cards out there. YouTuber Logan Paul famously blew over $5 million on a Pikachu Illustrator in 2022 and sold it in 2026 for $16 million, but that's just the tip of the iceberg.

We've searched online auction houses and scoured Pokémon history to find the 69 most valuable rare Pokémon cards ever sold (nice).

Because you're a true connoisseur, we know you'll want to read on for all those tasty, big money cards. But if you'd rather skip to the cream of the crop, hop straight to the top 10 most expensive Pokémon cards.

For details on how we track card sales for this guide, and expert tips on finding your own cards' value, you can also head to the FAQ section at the end of this guide.

These are the most expensive Pokémon cards:

69. Pokémon Card Fan Club Shining Magikarp

Price$14,000
Sale dateMay 24, 2023
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderBeckett
RatingGEM MT 9.5

Back in the early 90s, the Japanese Pokémon Card Fan Club (later succeeded by Pokémon Trainer's Card Magazine) advertised an extra-shiny Shining Magikarp promo. This fancy fish could only be won by obtaining 600 'GET points' at tournaments between 2000 and 2002.

As you can imagine, copies are fairly scarce. With so few available, it makes sense that a 9.5 gem mint copy fetched $14,000 on the auction site Fanatics Collect in 2023.

Functionally, the card is identical to Shining Magikarp from the regular 2002 Neo Genesis set. It has extremely similar art as well - you wouldn't know you had a gem at first glance.

What marks this Magikarp out from its school is the foiling. In the regular version, the background fish are shiny, whereas in the promo edition, it's the main, foreground Magikarp who shimmers. Just goes to show: when collecting rare Pokémon cards, the details matter.

68. Squirtle #29 Reverse Holo (Boundaries Crossed)

Price$15,000
Sale dateMarch 16, 2026
Auction houseEbay
GraderPSA
RatingPSA 10

Not all rare Pokémon cards start off rare. In fact, these days, it's not uncommon to see a pretty unremarkable card sell for silly money, merely because only a few people had the foresight to preserve a copy. 10+ years later, collectors will pay above the odds for one of the only top graded copies of that card in existence.

So it is with Squirtle #29 Reverse Holo from the 2012 set Boundaries Crossed. In late 2023, PriceCharting logged the sale of a PSA10 copy for just $250. But in March 2026, one sold for a princely $15,000 on Ebay, via the PSA Vault consignment service. That's a 5,900% increase in just over two years.

Reportedly, only two confirmed PSA 10 copies of the card exist, and the firms says it's only graded 37 copies at any grade - suggesting a vanishingly small pool of collectible-quality Squirtles out there. So it's certainly rare; only time will tell if paying 15 grand for this bathing cutie was a good investment.

67. First Edition Shining Charizard

Price$15,000
Sale dateOctober 30, 2022
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

One of the coolest Charizard cards ever printed, Shining Charizard from 2000's Neo Destiny set features a black shiny 'zard, with a foil treatment making the Pokémon literally 'shine'. Shining Pokemon were introduced in the previous set, Neo Revelation, and were very hard to get hold of, found in one pack in every 300 on average.

That scarcity was also reflected in the game's rules too. You were limited to only having one of each Shining card in your deck.

While still a darn sight less rare than their video game equivalents, Shining Pokémon in Neo Genesis were not common, so first edition versions that have remained in mint condition are now extremely scarce. The most expensive example of the card we found was this version, sold on eBay in January 1, 2025. It was originally listed for $17,999, but tracking sites like 130point claim the final selling price was $15,000.

66. Base Set First Edition Holo Mewtwo

Price$15,000
Sale dateApril 16 2023
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

For a certain generation of Pokémon fans, Mewtwo is the rare Pokémon, the rightful recipient of their Master Ball for (I probably threw mine at the first elemental bird I came across). It's unsurprising, then, that a card featuring the character would be worth something. Even more unsurprising is the fact it's the Base Set Shadowless 1st Edition Holo Mewtwo.

This card has everything - nostalgia, rarity, and a holographic background. It's also a shadowless card, meaning it was part of the first print run of the first English language Pokémon set. The most expensive copy we've seen sell is this PSA 10 copy sold via a Fanatics Collect auction in 2023.

65. Mega Charizard Y Poncho-wearing Pikachu

A rare Pokemon card depicting Pikachu wearing a cute little Poncho

Price$16,500
Sale dateSeptember 3 2026
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Mega Charizard Y Poncho-wearing Pikachu was one of two promo cards in a special box set released only in Japan on January 1. The contents were pretty similar to those of an elite trainer box, except of course for this utterly adorable Pikachu, dressed up like the then new Mega Charizard Y.

64. Espeon Gold Star

Price$22,100
Sale dateFebruary 2021
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Get used to seeing the phrase 'gold star' when it comes to rare Pokémon cards. Essentially an evolution of the Shining Pokémon concept, gold star cards likewise show the alternate color 'shiny' variant of the Pokémon they depict - which is why this Espeon is green.

Few gold star Pokémon cards are ever printed - on average you'd find one in every two booster boxes, or 1/72 packs. This, and the fact they often feature gorgeous art of fan-favorite Pokémon, makes them extremely coveted.

Espeon Gold Star is a stunning example of this. Released in the promotional POP Series 5 set of 2007, this card regularly sells for thousands of dollars. A 2021 auction on eBay set the record high price of $22,100 for a PSA 10 copy.

Still, it's not the most valuable Eeveelution of that set - you'll learn more about that soon.

63. Gengar VMAX

Price$23,400
Sale dateAugust 2026
Auction houseeBay
GraderBGS
RatingBlack Label 10

The alt art version of Gengar VMAX from 2021's Fusion Strike was one of the set's most sought-after chases - unsurprising given the charismatic art for the popular Pokémon - but it's the Japanese version printed in the earlier High Class Deck that's achieved higher prices. As reported on social media by TCG Collectr, in August 2026 a BGS Black Label 10 copy of the Japanese card sold for $23,400 on eBay. The grading made a huge difference to the price, since a (comparatively lowly) PSA 10 that sold around the same time went for a "mere" $2,600.

62. HG&SS Undaunted Umbreon

Price$25,000
Sale dateMay 04, 2026
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Amidst all the special variants, errors cards, and promos you'll see on this list, it's kind of refreshing to have this entry, which is just a card featuring a Pokémon that people really like. Umbreon has almost as many diehard fans as Charizard. It's got a badass but cute design, it released in Gen 2 so there's plenty of nostalgia there, and it's an Eeveelution to boot.

In the modern era of the Pokémon TCG, we're pretty used to Umbreon SIRs being among a set's biggest chase cards, but it's even more true for older, rarer cards. This Umbreon, hailing from 2010's Undaunted set, sold in 2026 for $25,000 via eBay.

61. Japanese Basic No Rarity Symbol Holo Poliwrath

Price$25,015
Sale date2020
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The 1996 Japanese Basic No Rarity Symbol Holo Poliwrath appeared in the original Pokémon base set, released in Japan in. Poliwrath isn't as widely popular as Charizard or Pikachu. Not quite the cutest Pokémon or the coolest, it's a bit of a sleeper in the original Pokédex. But every Pokémon is somebody's favorite.

At any rate, no collector in their right mind would turn down a PSA 10 card from the OG glory days of the Pokémon TCG. Proving our point, a 2020 auction from Fanatics Collect saw the water Pokémon sell for $25,015.

We should mention that the missing rarity symbol isn't a printing error, but a sign of authenticity. The first printings of first edition Pokémon cards in Japan lacked the symbol in the bottom corner. Japan didn't have shadowless cards, but these are essentially the equivalent.

60. 2009 Japanese Design Promo Spikey Eared Pichu

Price$25,800
Sale dateJune 2023
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

In 2009, as a promotion for the movie 'Arceus and the Jewel of Life', the Japanese publishing company Shogakukan held a drawing contest for children and young teens. Contestants were asked to share artwork for Arceus or Spikey-Eared Pichu, with the winners being turned into actual Pokémon cards. This delightful floral Pichu was designed by the second-grade winner, who was around seven or eight years old at the time.

According to Dicebreaker, only 13 to 100 copies of this card are thought to exist, and only three copies of Spikey-Eared Pichu have ever been graded by PSA. It's no wonder, then, that the 2009 Japanese Design Promo 2nd Grade Winner Spikey-Eared Pichu card can fetch such a high price, with a Fanatics Collect auction reaching $25,800 in June 2023.

59. Gold Pikachu

Price$29,520
Sale dateSeptember 2021
Auction houseGoldin
RatingEX 5

Nothing screams expensive like a flash of gold. And in this case, gold beats old. The Gold Pikachu Pokémon card was released in 2016, to mark the 20th anniversary of the Pokémon TCG.

Made of 11 grams of solid 24-karat gold, the card is a replica of the original Japanese Pikachu card's design, featuring a very round yellow mouse. To grab the card on release, buyers first entered a lottery, with winners given the chance to buy the limited edition card for a cool ¥216,000 ($2,000 / £1,700).

Since then, its value has risen swiftly. It sold for close to $8,000 (£5,750) in 2019, then $12,655 in 2020. Most recently, a version of the card went for a cool $29,520 in 2021. Notably, this was graded at EX 5 by PSA, so higher-priced Pikachu's are certainly possible

Although not legal in tournament play, the card came with a handy glass frame to display the artifact to visitors. You'd probably have to explain why spending nearly 30 grand on a single, unusable card was a good financial decision, though.

58. Darkrai #BW73

Price$30,000
Sale dateApril 27, 2026
Auction houseEbay
GraderPSA
Rating10

These days, nothing seems to send a Pokémon card's price rocketing quite like its featured 'Mon becoming the mascot of a brand new expansion. Consequently, the reveal of new Japanese set Abyss Eye, in April 2026, sent high-rolling collectors scrambling for high graded copies of older Darkrai cards.

Top of the pile is the remarkably imposing-looking 2013 Black & White promo card Darkrai #BW73, which sold in PSA 10 for a record price of $30,000 on Ebay, in the same month Abyss Eye was unveiled.

That's a staggering markup from the previous PSA 10 sale we found just two months before - a comparatively casual $15k - and more than three times the one before that, which fetched 'only' $8,700 in late 2025. This for a card from 2013's Team Plasma box which at the time retailed for 20 bucks.

57. X/Y 20th Anniversary Festa Pikachu

Price$32,250
Sale dateSeptember 3 2023
Auction houseGoldin
GraderBeckett
RatingPristine 10

While the Japanese X/Y 20th Anniversary Festa Pikachu is pretty recent as far as rare Pokémon cards go, it has a classic feel that older fans will still adore. It helps that all three Gen 1 starter Pokémon - plus the biggest icon of the IP, Pikachu - feature in its vibrant, adorable artwork.

This pricey piece of paper was given out to attendees of the 2016 Anniversary Festa in Toki Messe, Niigata, which took place to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the first-ever Pokémon game.

Its abilities aren't likely to win you tournaments, but they are pretty unique. A 120-damage attack 'Mega Thunderbolt' causes you to discard all Pikachu's energy, and the Celebration ability demands that every player clap their hands and then draw a card.

The highest-selling copy of this card was sold on March 9, 2023 via auction site Goldin. This card, given Beckett's maximum grade of 10 (Pristine), fetched $32,520 at auction.

56. Shining Mew CoroCoro Promo

Price$33,000
Sale dateJanuary 17, 2025
Auction houseeBay
GraderARS
Rating10

Featuring a lovely, baby blue Shiny Mew, this Japanese Shining Mew CoroCoro promo card is incredibly hard to get hold of. It's one of Japan's unnumbered promo cards, which have short print runs attached to specific events like tournaments and film releases.

In this case, Shining Mew was a promo card released in the May 2001 issue of a magazine, the kids manga CoroCoro. As you might expect for a freebie given out in a children's comic, few copies survived in good nick. Which is why a version of this Japanese card sold in January 2025 for a whopping $33,000.

55. 2002 Trophy Card Neo Summer Battle Road No. 2 Trainer

Price$34,100
Sale dateMarch 2021
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderBeckett
Rating7.5 NRMT

The 2002 Trophy Card Neo Summer Battle Road No. 2 Trainer is a card with a real mouthful of a name. But I'm sure its owner finds its value more than makes up for this.

The 2002 TCNSBRN2T (as we won't be calling it) was the second-place prize in the Junior Division of 2002's Kanto Summer Battle Road tournament. The recipient of this promo was Fukinishi Tomoki - a fact we know because their name and the region they competed in are printed on the card.

Prize promo cards, especially those with a unique name on them, are extremely hard to come by. For example, the priciest copy of this card was sold via Fanatics Collect in March 2021 for a cool $34,100, despite having a middling grade of 7.5 Near Mint.

54. Topps Chrome Charizard Tekno #06

Price$35,000
Sale dateAugust 27 2023
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
Rating10

Back in the 2000s, collectibles manufacturer Topps held the coveted Pokémon TCG production license. Among the early cards it produced was Topps Chrome Charizard Tekno #06, a particularly rare and particularly shiny card featuring one of the game's most popular 'mons.

Topps produced three types of shiny Pokémon cards, and of the three, Tekno-Chrome cards had the rarest pull rates. This means this Charizard was hard to hunt down at the time it was printed - nowadays, copies of this vintage card are even more scarce.

The highest sale price on record for a Tekno Topps Charizard can be found on Price Charting, which records an eBay sale from August 2023 of $35,000. The pristine quality of this card, which was graded a 10 by PSA, has clearly helped push up the price.

53. First Edition Holo Crystal Charizard

Price$40,800
Sale dateOctober 16 2022
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

While it's not the most popular card featuring this iconic Pokémon, the Holographic Crystal Charizard is pretty unique. It's an e-card that, when scanned with an e-reader, reveals bonus content like mini-games or Pokédex info.

This was a novelty that didn't stick around long. Mysterious Mountains (the set that Holo Crystal Charizard hails from) was the last Japanese expansion to include e-cards. It, along with its English-language equivalent Skyride, was also the last set produced by Wizards of the Coast before the publisher's Pokémon license ran out.

All this makes the card a rare and interesting part of Pokémon history. Combine that with the fact it's a Charizard Pokémon card, and you've got a recipe for high value. So far, the most we've seen Crystal Charizard sell for is $40,800 (£32,300) in an auction from October 2022.

52. Holo Gold Star Torchic

Price$43,200
Sale dateOctober 2021
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
RatingGEM MT 10

Printed gold star cards are hard to come by, and well-preserved copies are even rarer. That's what makes the Holographic Gold Star Torchic so expensive - PSA has so far recorded that only 19 copies with the pristine GEM MT 10 grade exist. It was one such gem that sold in April 2022 for $43,200 (£34,200).

Gold star cards are popular for their rarity, but their gorgeous art is also part of the appeal. Masakazu Fukuda's adorable rendition of Torchic, popping out of the frame with a cheeky wink and a flash of glitter, is sure to drive up the sentimental and fiscal value of the card.

51. Pikachu MTG Stock Test Proof

Price$45,000
Sale dateJune 2025
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
RatingPSA Authentic

It turns out that one of the most expensive Pokémon cards ever sold was actually a Magic: The Gathering card. Pikachu MTG Stock Test Proof is evidence that Wizards of the Coast did some printer testing before releasing its Base Set.

Here, we can see the adorable, chubby Pikachu from said set, printed on the back of an entirely unrelated TCG card. That happens to be Independent Troops from the Magic: The Gathering set Portal Three Kingdoms. Despite being printed on the back, Pikachu remains legible, vibrant, and as cute as ever.

This is certainly one of the more unique Pokémon cards, as it represents a bit of the game's history. It's also the only authenticated copy of the card to exist. That, no doubt, is why it sold for almost $50,000 at auction.

50. 2000 Tropical Mega Battle No. 1 Trainer

Price$48,125
Sale dateSeptember 2023
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
GraderCGC
RatingPristine 10

These promo cards were awarded to first-place winners of Japan's regional tournaments in 2000, which also saw the victors qualify for that year's Tropical Mega Battle tournament. Two versions of this promo card actually exist, depicting a male or a female trainer, and they were reportedly awarded to contestants based on their gender.

A precursor to more established competitive Pokémon competitions, Tropical Mega Battle took place annually in Hawaii between 1999 and 2001, and was the first major international competition for young Pokémon TCG fans. The competition included American and Japanese children (more countries were added after the first year) but only Japanese kids got these trophy cards.

Heritage Auctions claims that this copy of 2000 No. 1 Trainer Tropical Mega Battle is the only one to receive a Pristine 10 rating from CGC. However, despite its excellent condition, other, rarer trainer promos have sold for far higher prices.

49. Holo Gold Star Rayquaza

Price$48,958
Sale dateJune 1 2023
Auction houseCOLLECTR
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

EX Deoxys is one of the rarest Pokémon packs of all time, and Holographic Gold Star Rayquaza is its biggest chase card. Like all the rare gold star cards, this features a shiny Pokémon, and the card has a holographic sparkle. But few gold star Pokémon cards are as coveted as the stylish black and gold shiny Rayquaza.

This rare card from 2005 sold for a whopping $45,100 (£35,867) in 2020. We thought it may have peaked in value - as much more recently, a PSA 10 copy of the card went for just $38,100 (£30,300) - but apparently not, as on June 1, 2023, Rayquaza sold again for $48,598.

48. Master Scroll

Price$50,000
Sale dateAugust 2020
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The 2010 Master Scroll Trophy Card was an award given to the most dedicated members of the Japanese Pokémon fan club, the Daisuki Club.

The Daisuki Club was responsible for distributing promo cards to players between 2007 - 2010, after the Player's Club shut down. Fans could earn 'Action Points' through various activities, quizzes, and competing in tournaments, and the Master Scroll promo was the grand prize, given only to those who earned 8,600 points.

A grade 9 Master Scroll sold on eBay for somewhere in the ballpark of $50,000 (£40,000) (though it was an accepted offer, so we can't be sure of an exact price).

While the Daisuki Club still persists to this day, it no longer gives out unique promos.

47. 1999 Tropical Mega Battle No. 2 Trainer

Price$50,300
Sale date2020
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingAuthentic

The Tropical Mega Battle No. 2Trainer prize card was issued to the second place prize winner in 1999's Mega Battle Tournament, a seven-tournament grand slam culminating in a finals in Hawaii. The prize cards, which auctioneer Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC) states were given to the top three players from each region, all featured Exeggutor - a reference to the tournament's location.

Hardly any copies of this card have ever been professionally graded, so their rare auction appearances command a high price, regardless of how well preserved they are.

46. Wonder Platinum Japan National Championship Promo

Price$51,250
Sale dateDecember 2023
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The Wonder Platinum Japan National Championship Promo was given to competitors in the 2009 Japan World Championship representative Pokémon tournament. Winners of this national tournament would then be put forward for the 2009 World Championships. Only 20 copies were ever handed out, meaning this is an incredibly rare prize card.

While there's no adorable or epic Pokémon in its artwork, Wonder Platinum still features some quality illustration. Plus, the name is a reference to 2008's Pokémon Platinum.

45. Mega Charizard X ex Black Label

Price$54,100
Sale dateMarch 2026
Auction houseEbay
GraderBeckett
RatingBGS 10 Black Label

Pokémon card grading - paying a company money to measure every micron of your card and officially rate how perfect it is out of ten - is now crucial to the value of high-end cards. Half a point up or down on your grading can make thousands, tens of thousands, or in a few cases over a million dollars' worth of difference to the price.

Arguably the most extreme and exacting (and therefore desirable) grading for a card to get is Beckett's coveted 'Black Label' - which requires a perfect 10 on all four of the company's key metrics: surface, edges, corners, and centering.

Achieving that almost impossible, unicorn quality standard is what, in March 2026, transformed a copy of Phantasmal Flames' Mega Charizard X ex from an $800 card (very respectable, for a modern chase that only came out four months prior) to one that sold for over $54,000, winning it a seat in this all-time hall of fame.

44. Base Set First Edition Holo Chansey

Price$55,000
Sale date2020
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The 1999 Base Set 1st Edition Shadowless Holo Chansey is an original Pokémon card depicting a unique and popular Pokémon. It may be no Charizard, but Chansey has plenty of fans nonetheless and - perhaps surprisingly - is one of the most expensive Base Set cards, at least in good condition.

A PSA 10 Chansey card is very hard to come by. It's that holographic finish on the card - it scratches very easily. The lighter background makes those scratches show up more clearly and so, of the 16 holo cards from Base set, Chansey is by far the hardest to find in PSA 10 condition.

It's also theorized that early Pokémon players may have been prejudiced against the pink, nurturing Chansey Pokémon, and may have taken less good care of the card than they did with favorites like Charizard or Venusaur.

The highest sale of such a card for quite some time was $36,877 in October 2020, but then in July 2024 it was topped with an eye-watering $55,000 sale!

43. Base Set No Rarity Venusaur

Price$55,000
Sale date2021
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

First edition Pokémon cards are already a winner. And while Venusaur doesn't have the same pull as Charizard, this starter evolution still does stonks on the secondary market.

Base Set No Rarity Venusaur is made even more valuable because of a printing problem - the black star in the bottom right that's meant to denote the card's rarity, is missing. Oh, and this one in particular has the protective case signed by artist Mitsuhiro Arita. All in all, that led to a price of $55,000 (£43,700) at a PWCC auction in 2021 - though since the auctioneer has rebranded as Fanatics Collect the listing has gone from the site.

42. 64 Mario Stadium Snap Articuno

Price$58,560
Sale dateJuly 2024
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingCGC Pristine 10

One of a number of entries on this list from the Pokémon Snap contest run in 1999, this card was made thanks to a competition run by the Nintendo-focused Japanese TV show 64 Mario Stadium. Participants were asked to send in their greatest Pokémon snapshots from the game, and the best five were made into real Pokémon cards. The manga magazine CoroCoro Comic ran the same competition - also creating five cards.

Prerelease Raichu looks fairly innocuous: a base set Raichu with a prerelease stamp, similar to that found on the prerelease Clefable given out as a prize at early Wizards of the Coast events. But Raichu was never given out as a prize card - in fact it shouldn't really exist, and for many years it was dismissed as an urban legend.

We've got a separate article that explains the full history, and how it came to light. Here's the short version. In 1999 when WotC was getting ready to make the prerelease Clefable card, the initial version of the print sheet contained a small number of base set Raichus as well as the Clefables. The error was caught during production proofing and corrected, so only a tiny number of the Raichus were ever made, either eight or eleven according to different versions of the story.

All the copies of the card went home with Wizards of the Coast employees, who held onto them and occasionally teased fans by showing them off at public events. It wasn't until 2006 that they were confirmed to exist, and not until 2023 until any of the cards were graded. And so far as we know, a 2025 sale of one of the cards for $550,000 is the only time they've ever changed hands!

5. First Edition Base Set Holo Charizard

Price$700,000
Sale date 2026
Auction housePrivate
GraderTAG
RatingGEM MT 10

Ah, First Edition Base Set Holo Charizard. Ask a casual fan what the most sought-after Pokémon card is, and there's a good chance they'll answer: first edition shadowless Charizard. Perennially popular since its release in 1999, holographic Charizards have been a staple on the wish lists of collectors and fans for over 20 years, and a legend of playgrounds everywhere.

The first edition holo Charizard is particularly valued for its age, limited availability, and the recognizable image of one of Pokémon's much-loved mascots. Like all first edition Pokémon cards, this card is shadowless, printed without the dark border on the frame that was added later. There are a very few shadowless cards that aren't first edition, but it's the combination of the shadowless border and first edition logo that's the real certification of excellence.

In October 2020, a PSA 10 mint condition first-edition shadowless holographic Charizard was bought by ex-rapper Logic at auction for a sizeable $220,000 (£173,000), only to be surpassed a month later when another Charizard of the same specifications sold for $295,000 (£210,000).

A mint PSA 10 copy sold in 2022 for $420,000 (£334,000) via Fanatic Collect (formerly PWCC Marketplace) - but in April 2026, Collectr reported a private sale from Benjamin Be to Thiago Nigro for $700,000. That makes the First edition Charizard, once again, the most expensive playable Pokémon card in the world.

4. Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer

Price$1,769,000
Sale dateMay 18, 2026
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

It might feel odd for the third prize Trophy Pikachu card from the Pokémon TCG's earliest Japanese tournaments to sell for four times as much as the second prize card did in 2023. That's especially true, given both cards had the same perfect PSA 10 grading, both have a similar, vanishingly small population of PSA graded cards, and both were the only PSA 10 copy known to be in existence at the time of sale.

But that's exactly what happened: in May 2026, New Jersey auctioneers Goldin (yes, the ones from TV) sold the single confirmed Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer for a winning bid of $1.45 million - totalling 1,769,000 bucks after a 22% buyer premium. Why the huge price difference? Maybe the buyer liked the adorably tiny trophy; maybe the bronze sparkly finish simply looks a bit more like the gold of the No. 1 trophy card below.

Or maybe, in between 2023 and 2026, Pokémon cards have begun attracting so much more attention from the ultra-wealthy that the very rarest specimens are now a fashionable status symbol for billionaires (or those who wish to appear to be billionaires) to flaunt at each other.

Maybe the top end of this is mostly an ego playground for fabulously rich men who'll happily spend $1.77m - the cost of 4.1 million meals for starving people, according to the World Food Programme - on a 2.5 by 3.5 inch rectangle of cardboard, just because they can. Does it bring them as much joy as it brought a Japanese teenager at the end of one triumphant weekend in the late 90s? We can only imagine.

3. Trophy Pikachu No. 1 Trainer

Price$3,000,000
Sale dateSeptember 12, 2025
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingMINT 9

Sitting right at the top of the Trophy Pikachu Tree, fittingly, is 1998's Trophy Pikachu No.1 Trainer - extremely limited promos handed only to the winning Pokémon players at the TCG's second-ever sanctioned tournament, the 1997-98 Japanese Lizardon Mega Battle Pokémon competition.

Just like its promo prize siblings, the number-one Pikachu was illustrated by Mitsuhiro Arita. This time, the world's most popular Pokémon is lifting a trophy in the air, grinning in triumph.

Supposedly, there are only 14 copies of this card, period. We've seen others sell for thousands upon thousands, but none have quite matched the price of the copy sold in September 2025. It's understandable - MINT 9 might be the best grading we've ever seen this promo get. No.1 Trainer Pikachu is a true winner, indeed.

2. Raincoat Pikachu - perhaps

Price$8,400,000
Sale dateSeptember 28, 2026
Auction houseFanatics Collect
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Raincoat Pikachu was created as a prize for a competition tied to the 3DS game Pokémon Art Academy in 2015; fans had to draw Pikachu in the game and upload it to the Miiverse social network. Six winners each got 100 copies of the promotional Pikachu card featuring their very own illustration.

This is a rare card to be sure, and in September 2026 a copy sold for a massive $8,400,000 (including buyer's premium) on Fanatics Collect - at least, it seems like it did. There's actually some doubt.

Reporters at Chase Society noticed that this auction listing was removed from Fanatics Collect entirely, which is usually a sign that the buyer has failed to pay. The listing then returned to the site. As of November 13 2026 it's still up, but scrutinizing the page source data shows that it has the "cancelled" status. There's an error in the data, it's just not clear where, so we're keeping an eye on this one.

1. Pikachu Illustrator

Price$16,492,000
Sale dateFebruary 16, 2026
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The new holy grail of the TCG, Pikachu Illustrator is a promo Pokémon card originally handed out to winners of a 1998 illustration competition run through Japanese magazine CoroCoro. Only 39 copies were ever created.

It's the only card to feature the 'Illustrator' title instead of 'Trainer'. The artwork was drawn by esteemed Pokémon illustrator Atsuko Nishida, creator of Pokémon's main mascot, Pikachu. There's even a unique pen icon in the bottom-right corner, seen on no other card.

It's unknown exactly how many Pikachu Illustrator cards are still in existence, but ten PSA certified copies have been graded as 'mint'. From January 2021 onwards, it was the most expensive Pokémon card to ever be sold at auction, with a PSA 9 Mint condition card selling for a whopping $233,000 (£167,600).

Though it lost the title briefly, in July 2021 Logan Paul (yeah, that guy) spent $4 million on the only existing PSA 10 version of the card, getting the purchase accredited by Guinness World Records as the most expensive Pokémon card ever sold. But the value of the card was actually even higher: to secure the trade, Paul also handed over a lesser PSA 9 version of the card, which he'd previously purchased for $1,275,000.

The saga of this card doesn't end there. In early 2026, Mr Paul went on to sell the card to one AJ Scaramucci, once again getting Guinness involved. That's because the sales figure this time was a frankly staggering $16,492,000.

We should add that Logan also parted ways with the diamond-encrusted necklace he'd been carrying the card around in (does a $1 card taped to a $2 million car cost $2,000,001?) But even so, it's more than fair to call this the most expensive Pokémon card of all time!

It's a pity it's so rare: Pikachu looks even cuter than usual holding an oversized fountain pen.

Bonus - Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack

Price$2,700
Sale dateUnverified
Auction houseeBay
RatingN/A

We're including a bonus curiosity because it's just too interesting not to mention. When Wizards of the Coast realized they had accidentally printed too many Base Set booster packs branded with the first-edition logo, they covered the errant symbol with a small black triangle. A simple attempt to avoid wasting resources has generated a much-prized collector's item, as fans now clamor for a rare Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack.

It's the packaging itself that's valuable here, not the cards inside, so don't go cracking one of these black triangle packs open if you happen to find one sitting in the back of a drawer (you lucky devil).

They're occasionally found in standard Base Set booster boxes - so if you have one you'll have to weigh up whether to gamble on the chance discovery of one of the black triangle booster packs, or whether it's best to leave the box unopened for its pristine value. Some of the black triangle boosters have fetched over $2,700 (£2,000) on eBay, depending upon their condition and which Pokémon is displayed on their cover.

Rare Pokémon cards FAQ

How we find the most expensive Pokémon cards

To compile this list, we come back each month to trawl the latest sales on global trading card and collectibles auction houses like Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC), Heritage Auctions, and Goldin Auctions. We aim to keep the rankings and prices as up to date as possible.

Remember that, like all collectibles and investments, the Pokémon card market is very volatile, and prices can change fast and often. If you're looking to buy and sell high value Pokémon cards, you need to take care to double check the latest prices, being very conscious of the website or auction house's commission rates and fees.

Which Pokémon cards are rarest?

The most valuable Pokémon cards normally command high prices because they're old and there are very few copies in circulation. Most originate from the earliest Pokémon sets, or are one-off tournament prize cards printed in very low numbers. First edition Pokémon cards, peculiar misprints, and desirable old promos all fetch very high prices.

How to tell if a Pokémon card is rare?

Wargamer has a dedicated guide to Pokémon card rarity covering the basic rarity levels of cards you can open in any pack. If you think an old card you've gotten hold of could be particularly valuable, our guides to first edition Pokémon cards and shadowless Pokémon cards will help you to identify them. It's also worth referring to our guide to fake Pokémon cards, as there are plenty of counterfeits on the market.

How to sell rare Pokémon cards

We have a dedicated guide on how to sell Pokémon cards, so we recommend you read that if you're considering trading - but here's the short version.

If you think you're holding a truly valuable Pokémon card, your first port of call is to get it protected by placing it in a thin, soft-plastic sleeve, then into a protective, hard-plastic 'toploader' case. Before spending any more money on the card, it's usually a good idea to show it to an expert in-person, to get their opinion on its condition and potential value. A specialist at your local games store may be able to help.

Then you should get it graded by a well-regarded, expert grading service - PSA Pokémon card grading is the most popular in the USA. Once you get the card back with an official grading from 1 to 10, and stored in a professional PSA protective case, you should have a good idea what price range you're likely to get for it.

Bear in mind that there's usually a huge difference in value between a PSA grade 7, 8, or 9 card (generally mint condition to the naked eye) and a perfect PSA 10 card (absolutely faultless, even when viewed under a microscope from every angle). The really high prices paid by top level collectors are only for PSA 10 cards, and a PSA 10 is very often worth more than twice as much as the exact same card at PSA grade 8 or 9.

If you don't find any ultra-valuable Pokémon cards in your collection, it's really not the end of the world. This is a game, remember - what you have got is a delightful collection to treasure and play with. If you want to share any new pack pulls or treasured classics with a community of fellow fans, you're most welcome in the Wargamer Discord!

To keep up to date with the latest news about new rare cards and any bargains we find, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.
