title: The best Warhammer 40k games
content:
From tabletop-flavored strategy titles to grungy first person shooters, Games Workshop's grimdark universe has spawned over 70 videogames since Warhammer 40,000 first hit tabletops in 1987. Many of them have, sadly, sucked - but we 40k fans are nothing if not persistent. Gathered for your edification, these are the best Warhammer 40,000 games you can play right now, from recent releases to retro classics.

To dive into our experts' top rated Warhammer 40k videogames - chosen from team Wargamer's all time favorite strategy, action, and story driven 40k games - just read on. Alternatively, we've got the latest info on upcoming 40k games like Total War 40k and Dawn of War 4 - and finally the complete list of all 40k videogames released since 1987, for the history buffs. Just use the links below to find what you need!

The best Warhammer 40k games are:

  • Space Marine 2
  • Rogue Trader
  • Boltgun
  • Darktide
  • Chaos Gate Daemonhunters
  • Dawn of War
  • Warhammer Survivors
  • Battlesector
  • Battlefleet Gothic Armada 2
  • Mechanicus
  • Space Hulk Tactics
  • Dawn of War 2
  • Gladius Relics of War
  • Space Marine
  • Sanctus Reach
  • Final Liberation: Epic 40,000
  • Shootas Blood & Teef
  • Eternal Crusade
  • Inquisitor Martyr
  • Upcoming games
  • Full list
  • FAQ

1. Space Marine 2 (2024)

Saber Interactive / Focus Entertainment

We waited 13 years for a sequel to the 2011 third-person shooter Space Marine, and it wasn't in vain. Warhammer 40k Space Marine 2 hits like a 121-tonne Thunderhawk gunship, offering by far the most visually spectacular 40k videogame ever seen, and femur-shattering combat that
takes the original's genius gameplay and turns it up to 11 (or XI, in Warhammer terms).

Blasting and tearing through hordes of Tyranids and warp-teleporting warbands of Thousand Sons Chaos Space Marines is an ultraviolent delight, and the varied weapons offer a rich selection of methods for eviscerating them. Missions are almost uniformly fantastically designed, and every boss fight is a challenging treat.

The main story is a damp squig, with plenty of explosive set-pieces but not much charisma from the heroes or the villains. A combo of built-for-multiplayer design and dumb AI squadmates make the campaign a real trial to play on your own - we can't recommend this for single player purists.

But if you've got pals to play with (or don't mind matchmaking with randos) SM2's interwoven modes of co-op campaign, PVE Operations missions, and PVP multiplayer matches are fantastic. We really can't overstate how much fun that core combat is, either. This is by far the best Warhammer 40,000 action game yet made.

And the DLC has all been really good - well, except for that one voice pack so bad they refunded everyone who bought it. Battle passes aren't time-limited, so there's no real FOMO, which is by far the most consumer friendly way to monetize this kind of content. It's also been accompanied by a trove of free missions, weapons, and even gameplay modes - Space Marine 2 continues to get better and cheaper.

Read our Warhammer 40k Space Marine 2 review.

2. Rogue Trader (2023)

Owlcat Games

No other game captures the immense scale of the Warhammer 40k universe like Rogue Trader. This isometric, party-based CRPG puts you in charge of a city-sized spaceship, and tasks you with building your own dynasty among the stars in a subsector ravaged by warpstorms.

Your custom character is one potential successor to a veteran Rogue Trader, a space-faring merchant queen with a divine mandate to expand the borders of the Imperium through trade and conquest. You won't wait in the wings for long, though - treachery and Chaos plots put your forebear out of the picture and you into the Captain's throne soon enough.

The adventure that follows will take you at least 100 hours to complete. To begin with, you'll be concerned with getting your city-sized void-ship into peak running order. But beyond that you have the conspiracy of your predecessor's murder to unravel, trade deals to broker, adventures tied to your NPC companions' backstories, and an empire to build.

A gamut of systems have been put in place to reflect your status as a profoundly wealthy and powerful individual. Building your trade Empire sometimes happens in story beats, like main-story-missions to make contact with lost worlds and kick their planetary governors into line. But there's a lightweight colony management minigame, in which you'll found settlements, extract resources from them, and shape their development as crises arrive.

Combat happens both in the void of space and in head to head ground fights. The ground combat is particularly visceral, enhanced by appropriately cacophonic audio design for iconic weapons like the boltgun and chainsword. It's enjoyably deep, too, with as many technical options to manipulate the battlefield and layer buffs and debuffs as there are OTT weapons.

To realize a game on this scale, developer Owlcat limited the scope in some areas. Rogue Trader's graphics are effective but unexceptional. The game launched with plenty of bugs, though these have mostly been squashed. It takes a traditional approach of thoroughly separating combat, dialogue, and exploration, and the environments are mostly set-dressing compared to the interactive arenas of Baldur's Gate 3.

But the heart and soul of the game is spot on. Rogue Trader has thousands of lines of dialogue, and the narrative leads absolutely get Warhammer 40k - the horror, inhumanity, and pathos of the Imperium of Man. This shines through particularly well in your NPC companions, who are written to be believably human, yet distinctively alien.

Read our Warhammer 40k Rogue Trader review.

3. Boltgun (2023)

Auroch Digital / Focus Entertainment

If you want to feel like an unstoppable juggernaut of destruction, play Boltgun. A first person shooter inspired by early FPS games like Quake and Doom, it's a game in which you go fast and shoot hordes of enemies into teeny tiny bits - and that's it.

The retro graphics, with sprite-based enemies and low-poly 3D arenas, are a mission statement: this is a pure retro FPS experience. Wearing the big stompy boots of Ultramarines Sternguard veteran Malum Caedo, you'll blast, jump, and chainsword your way through thousands of the followers of Chaos.

You're here to shoot stuff, and boy does shooting stuff feel great. The game's armory is realized with loving care and attention. They're lovingly realized as pixel models, but the audio feedback is where they really shin. The meltagun roars like Cerberus, the heavy bolter thunders like an industrial press, and destroyed enemies come apart with a sound like a beef carcass being thrown into an industrial fan.

It's not just vibes, though - there's surprising tactical depth behind your choice of weapons. Just like the tabletop game, weapons have a Strength score and enemies a Toughness score - you'll do only marginal damage if you attempt to hit a baddy with an outclassed weapon. Each enemy has a distinctive role in combat, from the hindering nuisance of the Nurglings to the killer deathrays of a Lord of Change.

While the graphics are simple, the level design is excellent, both visually and as combat arenas. Colossal forge complexes, Chaos transdimensional gateways, and the warped interior of a corrupted space-ship represent the massive scale of 40k beautifully - though an in-game map would have been very helpful on some of the more sprawling levels.

You get to explore those locations at high speed, with some movement conveniences that the Doomslayer and Mr Quake never had access to in the '90s. An automatic ledge grab and mantle climb make jumping a little easier; the bullrush charge lets you close rapidly on distant shooters and splat smaller foes entirely; and your chainsword attack can help you clear even greater distancers by pulling you magnetically towards your target. It all feels great.

Read our Warhammer 40k Boltgun review.

4. Darktide (2022)

Fatshark

If you're a fan of both co-op multiplayer FPS games and Games Workshop's grim, dark, bloodstained far future, Darktide will blow your mind (especially when playing as the psyker character, who can literally blow enemies' minds by exploding their heads with concentrated warp energy).

Warhammer 40k Darktide is effectively a 40k-flavored reincarnation of its bestselling co-op slash-em-up Vermintide 2, which was based in the Old World fantasy setting. You play a 'reject' part of an Imperial Inquisitor's warband, completing various missions in a hive city that's overrun with servants of the Chaos god Nurgle.

Each of the classes offers a different core ability and playstyle, its own variety of guns, armor, and wargear, and a different library of conversational voice lines that'll play out in procedurally generated conversations between the characters as you fight through waves of chaos-warped enemies, complete challenges, and fight disgusting bosses.

The voice lines can start to grate a little over time, but there's enough variety that it still works well (and it helps that the voice acting and writing are both excellent, with superstar Black Library author Dan Abnett on the team).

The game's environments are frequently stunning, an impressively faithful, atmospheric rendering of 40k's unique aesthetics. You'll be fighting through the spires and flying buttresses of futuristic gothic rooftops one mission, and trudging through oppressive, grimy industrial undercities the next. Until Space Marine 2 came out, it was the best simulation of the Warhammer 40k world we've seen in a videogame - and when it comes to really delving deep into the grotty underbelly of the Imperium, it remains unbeaten.

And you're not just constrained to the underhive any more! The recent Beyond the Hive expansion added the new Expedition mode which sends your rejects into the Deadside radzones. These massive open environments are almost a complete new game in their own right - open ended (dare we say 'open world?') environments with more than a hint of Helldivers about them. And there's a touch of extraction shooter in here too, as you'll have free reign about when you call the Valkyrie to haul your asses out of the fire. 

5. Chaos Gate Daemonhunters (2022)

Complex Games / Frontier Developments

Warhammer 40k Chaos Gate Daemonhunters just steals the crown from Mechanicus as the best game like XCOM set in the 40k universe. In Daemonhunters, you take command of a strike force of Grey Knights - an elite, secretive chapter of Space Marines that are all psykers - and use their psychic might and advanced wargear to combat incursions by Chaos Daemons.

You'll build a base, train and equip a team of soldiers, and deploy them on various missions to hold back an oncoming, apocalyptic threat - a new, deadly galactic plague cooked up by the Chaos god Nurgle.

The various different classes of Grey Knights available for your roster (as well as the Duty Eternal DLC's Venerable Dreadnought and Imperial Assassins in the Execution Force expansion) each offer different skill trees to upgrade and specialize throughout the game - so long as you keep them alive.

Combine that with a ton of unlockable weapons and wargear items, plus cosmetic customization options coming out the wazoo, and you've got a 'war-barbie' experience second only to collecting and painting miniatures in real life.

Like others in the genre, Chaos Gate Daemonhunters' race-against-time campaign is a tough strategic challenge, forcing you to manage limited resources and prioritize your missions carefully against a stronger, better-resourced, ever-growing opponent.

In a twist on the XCOM DNA, your superhuman Space Marines' shots will always hit their target (no soul-crushing percentage hit chances here) and you're given a lot of handy contextual information to inform your tactics before you commit to a movement.

But every few turns you'll hit a Warp Surge, which grants your Nurgle-loving enemies a random chaos boon. These range from temporary damage boosts to mid-game reinforcements. Missions reward quick thinking, aggressive tactics, and canny use of specialists' abilities; it's excellently done.

Like XCOM 2 before it, Daemonhunters can be an exhaustingly intense experience, where losses are all but inevitable. But the blend of strategy and tactics is on point, the core gameplay is very satisfying, and the Warhammer 40k lore well realized. If you like both XCOM and Warhammer, this is essential.

Read our Warhammer 40k Chaos Gate Daemonhunters review.

6. Dawn of War - Definitive Edition (2025)

Relic Entertainment / THQ

Back to the classics now: 2004's Dawn of War is a giant which still stands up as one of the best RTS games ever made. Though it pioneered many concepts that would drive the RTS genre forwards in more heroic, tactical directions, it remains rooted in the base-building RTS era.

Developer Relic struck gold by simplifying and streamlining many classic RTS mechanics. Infantry are spawned in easy to control squads, not individual figures that have to be cursor-lassoed together. Resources come from taking and holding battlefield strongpoints, not faffing with ancillary farmer units.

Base-building is lightweight, strongly focused on unlocking military units and upgrades. This game, like its tabletop counterpart, wants you to leave the admin at home, get out there, and make war.

More importantly than all of that, it gets the feel right. Dawn of War has just enough lore-appropriate flavour to sate players with a shelf full of lovingly painted Dark Angels right above their monitor, but not so much as to confuse others, or bog down the game's inherent strengths as a fast-paced, aggressive RTS.

Over its lifespan, Dawn of War acquired three chunky expansion packs, first Winter Assault, and then the expandalone Dark Crusade and Soulstorm. These added new singleplayer campaigns, new forces for multiplayer, and even a lightweight grand strategy layer that saw you battle for control of a whole planet. The game also attracted a sterling modding community, adding in missing armies and the largest, most ridiculous units - Imperial Titans.

There's a rock-solid gameplay foundation, but the original game is quite crunchy on the eyes. The memory limitations of the original 32-bit game engine also couldn't keep up with the ambitions of modders. But you don't have to play the original game any more - in 2025 Relic Entertainment released the Definitive Edition of Dawn of War.

Definitive Edition follows the original game so closely you might wonder what it's done - other than bundle in all the original expansions, and provided a welcome but hardly revolutionary graphical upgrade - to justify a modern price point.

That would be the complete rework of the game code to make it compatible with modern 64 bit computer systems. Not only does this future proof the game to keep it running on modern systems, it lets the game take advantage of the huge memory in modern PCs. Since the game is so close to the original version, it is largely compatible with existing mods, and becoming more so as the developers at Relic and mod makers work to close the gap. If there was ever a modding community that could use more RAM, it's the Dawn of War scene…

Warhammer Survivors (2026)

Aurochs Digital

Warhammer Survivors is a bullet heaven game with low-fi pixel art and a choice to play in either the Age of Sigmar and Warhammer 40k universe. Just like the genre-defining Vampire Survivors, your little hero faces off against waves and waves of encroaching enemies, turning them into skull-shaped experience gems that you can then turn into level-ups. Winning means selecting the right upgrades at the right time and getting ahead of the curve by building a synergistic arsenal of upgrades - long term success means discovering ever more obscure secrets hidden among the levels.

In our review, we found it to be so close to Vampire Survivors that we had to cap its grade at a seven out of 10; it's hardly innovating on a game that's already five years old. But it successfully copies both the charisma and obscenely compelling gameplay of that original, wraps it up in a Warhammery package, and continues to eat up our time. It's just great fun.

For more on Warhammer Survivors, see the Steam page.

8. Battlesector (2021)

Black Lab Games / Slitherine

As incurable tabletop 40k megafans, we are suckers for the concept of a turn-based PC wargame that nails not only the 40k vibe, but also the gamefeel of building and fighting tabletop armies - and that's exactly what the wargame maestros at Slitherine have created in Battlesector.

We had our issues with it on release, but there's no doubting its finely tuned, compulsive core tactical gameplay, as you carefully advance, position, and direct your specialized units, managing a careful balance of buffs and abilities to obliterate as many superbly recreated, grimdark baddies as possible every turn.

In the three years since release, developer Black Lab has tweaked and improved a massive amount of Battlesector's rougher edges - not to mention adding eight full new playable factions, from the pitiless metal Necrons to the high-tech mech-loving Tau Empire. If you want to play real-life 40k across a range of lovingly realized, atmospheric battlefields, Battlesector is the closest you're going to get - just get ready for many unplanned hours of 'one more turn'…

Read our Warhammer 40k Battlesector review.

9. Battlefleet Gothic: Armada 2 (2019)

Tindalos Interactive / Focus Home Entertainment

In the grim darkness of the 41st millennium, there is only war. But the vast majority of 40k games tend to focus on 'grounded' fighting, whether that be on the surface of embattled planets, inside the tossing, red-lit corridors of a freshly-boarded warship, or deep within the pitch-dark, drifting belly of a Space Hulk.

Not so amid the cosmic naval warfare of Battlefleet Gothic, first launched as a spaceship fleet-based miniatures game in 1999, and revived for PC by developer Tindalos in 2016, three years after the dwindling tabletop line was finally canned by Games Workshop; and the 2019 sequel is the best execution of strategic void warfare yet.

You take command of a flotilla of 40k's preposterous spacefaring warships: colossal, flying gothic cathedrals with more buttresses, spires, and crenellations than a small European city. You'll through fleet-on-fleet battles on a fixed horizontal plane, against vessels from a selection of humanity's many deadly enemies.

On top of that, there are three fully fledged campaigns in the base game. There's a certain level of 4x gameplay here, as you secure control over different systems and muster your armies, and while the Imperial campaign is the 'default', the Tyranid Hive Fleets and robotic Necrons both offer very interesting variants. The strategic value of a planet if fundamentally different when all you want to do is eat it, after all.

With their slow turning circles and prow-mounted broadsides, there's a lot in common between the Imperial Navy and 19th century ships of the line. But the many fleets of the Imperium and its enemies - both servants of chaos and alien xenos races - wage war in the void in starkly different ways, from the nimble and fragile Aeldari to the ram-fronted Ork ships, and as well as the three campaign factions there are loads more to tussle with in multiplayer or skirmish mode.

10. Mechanicus (2018)

Bulwark Studios / Casedo Games

The Adeptus Mechanicus is a faction of technology-worshipping cyborg mystics from Mars, whose prevailing mission is to amass hoards of technological wisdom and understanding - primarily by scouring the galaxy for rare, complex or esoteric gadgets, stealing them, and taking them home to tinker with in the garage for the rest of time.

This, in a nutshell, is the plot of Kasedo Games' 2018 turn-based tactical squad battler, Mechanicus. You take command of a small but growing squad of Adeptus Mechanicus tech-priests, tasked with exploring worlds in search of hi-tech plunder. So far, so good.

Once you get down to the surface, though, things start getting all spooky, geometric, green, and glowing real fast. Those subterranean treasure vaults you saw on the scanners were, it seems, actually stasis crypts full of Necrons - soulless, ancient robotic killers - and they are none too pleased to be woken up by a bunch of half-organic grave robbers trying to nick their laptops.

So begins your distinctly XCOM-inspired progression through a series of increasingly challenging - but quite similar - grid-based maps, carefully managing your tech-priests' limited action points to complete objectives, while avoiding vaporization in the neon green beams of Necron gauss weapons.

Mechanicus is here in no small part because of its strikingly faithful, vivid, and unapologetically weird portrayal of the Adeptus Mechanicus - a lovably eccentric but fairly high-concept sci-fi faction that it would have been so easy to deal with in a half-arsed way.

From the characters' campy, cyborg-ish names made up of jumbled numerals and Greek letters, down to the fizzling data-blurts of their part-sonic, part digital language, Kasedo did the AdMech properly.

If you like the sound of XCOM-like gameplay with a few smart twists, a surprisingly excellent narrative, battling cyber-mummies in a dusty crypt, and having USB sticks for fingers, this is the one for you.

11. Space Hulk: Tactics (2018)

Cyanide / Focus Entertainment

Games Workshop's original Space Hulk board game released in 1989 to some acclaim, pitting the Space Marines' elite Terminator warriors against scythe-clawed alien fiends in a lightless, terrifying cosmic shipwreck. It was "heavily inspired by" (lovingly riped-off from) James Cameron's Aliens, translating its paranoid sci-fi dungeons into the 40k universe.

Subsequent editions in 1996, 2009, and 2014 sold well to a growing cult audience, especially 2014's fourth edition, which arrived at the very start of Warhammer's recent renaissance. Space Hulk on the tabletop, therefore, has earned its place as one of Warhammer 40k's most distinguished and popular games. The digital adaptations? Not so much.

There are no fewer than eight videogames bearing the Space Hulk name (if you count its 2005 outing on the Nokia N-Gage), but none has made an impact anywhere near the scale of their board-based grandpappy - none, that is, except developer Cyanide's breakout 2018 adaptation, Space Hulk: Tactics.

The core of Tactics is a direct remake of the board game, adding characterful and well-observed 3D graphics to turn out a perfectly portable PC and console port. Around that core is a new system of cards to further customize your team of Blood Angels, granting them extra abilities that just might turn the tide of battle at the game's crucial moments.

The game even features twin campaigns; one the classic Blood Angel campaign against the Genestealers from the board game, the other a prequel set centuries earlier that flips the table to put you in control of the Tyranids against the Ultramarines. It's a single-player feast.

If you like 40k, slick digital board game adaptations, and spending multiple hours scant grid squares away from slavering alien bioweapons that want to eat your organs, you're in the right place. Recommended.

12. Dawn of War 2 (2009)

Relic Entertainment / THQ

In every Warhammer 40k videogames thread, a divide quickly forms between those reformists who prefer the squad-level, RPG-inspired narrative campaigns of Dawn of War 2, and the base-building competitive RTS purists, for whom the OG Dawn of War is a masterpiece, and the sequel an ill-considered damp squib.

Both the original Dawn of Wars are superb in their own right - but each lends itself to a very different style of play, and aims to create different kinds of experience for the player. Dawn of War 2 distils, streamlines, nips and tucks the RTS genre. Sprawling, wide-open maps are squeezed down into graphically lusher, but completely linear, railroaded environments.

The quickly-snowballing hordes of units you once flung across the map are replaced with just a couple of persistent squads, led by named characters, with RPG-like equipment upgrades, and skill progression mechanics. Base-building is all but erased from the game, buildings reduced to inert terrain pieces from which to respawn your (very limited) support units, should they fall.

You'll select from a choice of squads to take on each sortie, decking each warrior out with different wargear and skills to mix up their in-game tactics. Finding what works best for you is a whole ton of fun, and you'll soon develop favorite squads whether because of their tactical capabilities or simply their witty banter. Storytelling is entwined with the gameplay, not just delivered via cutscenes, making it a much more narratively coherent experience.

We could go on for pages about the innovative storytelling in DoWII, its beautifully-constructed missions, and the ingenious, maddeningly addictive and shockingly ahead-of-its-time Last Stand horde mode, but, honestly, your time would be better spent just playing the game. Just go and get it, right now. We mean it.

13. Gladius - Relics of War (2018)

Proxy Studios / Slitherine Studios

Where Warhammer 40k the tabletop miniature wargame puts you in charge of an army, Gladius - Relics of War puts you in charge of a complete military industrial complex. It's the only Warhammer 40k 4X game so far.

4X stands for Explore, Expand, Exploit and Exterminate, popularized by the Civilization franchise. This city-settling, infrastructure-building, 'one more turn' model of strategy is an odd fit for the violence-first world of Warhammer 40k, but Gladius works surprisingly well.

The visuals are gorgeous, if let down by some unremarkable and slightly immersion-breaking janky animations (it ain't no Civ in that department). Those hoping for hardcore wargame levels of mechanical depth will come away a little hungry hungry, but there's enough meat to the factions' tech trees and progression to provide a respectable, if quite easy-going strategy package overall.

While Civilization is the standard-bearer for the 4X genre, Gladius has much more in common with Endless Legends. The map is divided into regions, each of which can support just one city. As a city grows it expands into neighboring hexes, eating up their resources and producing specialized nodes. The birds-eye view tiny 40k cityscapes is a treat - as is blowing them up.

If you're a 40k fan who cut their gaming teeth on Civilization (on a lower difficulty setting, at least) don't sleep on Gladius; there's a lot of fun to be had here.

14. Space Marine (2011)

Relic Entertainment / THQ

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine, the epic, gore-drenched odyssey of Ultramarines Captain Titus achieves something Warhammer computer games almost never do: it actually makes us care about its main character. Not that this is a complicated tale - you go to a human factory planet besieged by Orks, kill thousands of Orks, realize it was Chaos' nefarious doing all along, kill the Chaos leader. Hardly Shakespeare.

No, we care about Titus because he's the most impressively realized, most relatable and believable Space Marine warrior ever in a videogame. By placing us in his massive ceramite boots, this game gets closer than any other to recreating on screen the peculiarly gripping power fantasy of being a transhuman Astartes warrior.

Titus' 8-foot-tall, 6-foot-wide bulk towers over human-sized NPCs and scampering greenskin enemies alike, making you feel like one of the magnificent gods of war so reverently described in Black Library novels. Every decibel of his voice - the inimitable and perfect booming tones of Mark Strong - projects the grave, dutiful assiduousness of an Ultramarine.

His every animated step, lunge, swing and leap is perfectly tuned to feel impossibly powerful and weighty. Titus is relentless and heavy, a freight train of a combatant.

The game's atmosphere is treacle-thick, bloody, and intoxicatingly 40K. While the environments are an endless succession of near-identical corpse-strewn industrial zones, it really doesn't matter, because all you'll care about is the banging of your boltgun's explosive shells and the rhythmic roar of your chainsword swinging up and down, carving Orks into green-and-red jelly.

Yes, Space Marine 2 is out now, and outstrips the 2011 original in most ways - but the first game saw a bump in sales since SM2 came out for a good reason.

But there are two blemishes on this otherwise deeply agreeable game. First, the original version of the game - now sold as Anniversary Edition - retails for a frankly silly price given its age. Then there's the slightly more expensive Master Crafted edition which has some big reliability issues.

15. Sanctus Reach (2017)

Straylight Entertainment / Slitherine

Another turn based battler, 2017's Sanctus Reach is a clear forerunner to Battlesector, in that you'll be assembling tabletop-style army lists, deploying your forces, and fighting it out over objective points. To be clear, it's not as new and pretty as Battlesector, its campaign missions and tactical mechanics aren't as varied or interesting, and there's less faction variety, particularly with Battlesector's healthy haul of DLC.

So why do we still recommend it as one of the best 40k games around? Firstly, it has some features Battlesector doesn't, which make it a different and worthwhile play. There's destructible terrain and cover that changes the battlefield as you go - and you'll also be ramping up to slightly larger battles, including titanic units like Imperial Knights and Orky Gorkanauts and Morkanauts, adding a sense of scale Battlesector lacks.

Secondly - and maybe we're just wearing rose-tinted specs here - as a 2017 release, it's one of the last 40k games to release before 8th edition, the return of Roboute Guilliman, and the advent of the Primaris Space Marines. Firstborn marines, in all their 90s-style stumpy glory, play the starring role here, alongside the classic Castraferrum 'box' Dreadnoughts that Games Workshop has since so cruelly slashed from the codex and its stores.

Oldmarines are still plentiful in Battlesector, and they're hardly done dirty - all have important tactical roles - but they're sometimes upstaged by your shiny new Inceptors, Aggressors, and Invictor Warsuits. If you love Battlesector and want something similar, but with a bit more scale and more of a retro 40k feel, Sanctus Reach is right up your alley.

16. Final Liberation: Epic 40,000 (1997)

Holistic Design Inc.

It's an empirically proven fact that Warhammer 40k videogames have gotten markedly better after the year 2000 than they were before it (we think it's because of y2k, but we can't prove it) - but there are exceptions to every rule, and Final Liberation is one of them.

Released in 1997 (that's after the printing press, but before the breakdown of the western liberal-democratic order, history fans), this is a strategic level computer wargame based on Epic, GW's late 90s 40k spinoff, which simulated much larger-scale battles and campaigns by using teeny, tiny 6mm scale figures, rather than the standard 28mm or 32mm-high guys.

Final Liberation sees you marshal a huge combined force of Ultramarines, Astra Militarum tanks and infantry, and tower-block sized Titans, and direct them across entire continents to fight off a colossal Ork Waaagh! through deadly but rewarding turn based tactical battles.

The 1990s are often remembered fondly as a 'golden age' of Warhammer 40k, driven by sheer bombast and silliness, rather than the mass market appeal of today's game. Final Liberation fits in perfectly, and it's required gaming for new 40k nerds wanting to sample the wildly different vibes of the before-times. But it's also, fundamentally, a compelling large-scale turn-based strategy game that'll have you hooked once you know the ropes.

If you try out Final Liberation and love fighting those larger scale battles, you should also check out Legions Imperialis - GW's new iteration of Epic, set in the Horus Heresy era and launched in 2023.

17. Shootas, Blood & Teef

Rogueside

Shootas, Blood & Teef is the least serious, most delightfully slapstick Warhammer 40k game on this list. This is a side-scrolling run and gun multiplayer platformer in the style of Metal Slug, Broforce, or even Castle Crashers. Up to four allied Orks set out on a violent quest to batter everything in their path with bullets, lasers, explosions, and weaponized squigs.

Developer Rogueside honed their craft for this type of gameplay with the Guns, Gore, and Cannoli series, and the look and feel of SBT is absolutely spot on. The chunky cartoon art style matches the over the top character of the Orks perfectly, and the huge Imperial war machines that appear in some boss fights, like the Baneblade or Knight Valiant, are fantastic.

We have to put a very big caveat here. The story campaign is short, probably around four hours long. There is team-based Ork on Ork multiplayer, with a variety of modes, but that relies on a stable player population.

However, the Steam version of the game has the great 'Remote Play Together' feature: only one player in a multiplayer group needs to buy a copy of the game for their friends to join a session. It's a lot easier to recommend this as a short-lived but high impact experience for a group of chums - you'll get more hours entertainment for much less cost than buying cinema tickets.

18. Eternal Crusade

Behaviour Interactive

Eternal Crusade is a contentious entry, as it is both no longer running and something of a disappointment. The first version of the Eternal Crusade website advertised "third person persistent online action in the first MMORPG of the 41st Millennium": but by the time of launch, the RPG part had entirely gone.

The Eternal Crusade we actually got was a match based multiplayer third-person shooter, with faction wins factoring into control of an overworld - a bit like Planetside, but without the persistent largescale warzones. Matches played out like Battlefield, with large forces going to war over massive maps that required transport vehicles to traverse.

It was fantastic - sometimes. Players unlocked new equipment and weapons at a snail's pace (unless you paid for microtransactions), which made for a serious balance problem given that only specialized equipment could reliably deal damage to vehicles.

But it had real highlights: the factions were extremely asymmetrical, the classes all felt like the familiar 40k units they represented, and the netcode for melee duels worked remarkably well. Then there were the multi-stage sieges, which had an excellent rhythm, and always ended in a hopeless (or triumphant) last stand.

The official servers are long dead. But there is an active 'Eternal Crusade Resurrection' community, which operates a fan reimplementation of the game and organizes matches via Discord.

19. Inquisitor: Martyr (2017)

NeoCore Games

Inquisitor: Martyr casts you as an agent of the Imperium's shadowy, pseudo-religious, paramilitary secret police force, the Holy Inquisition. Arriving aboard a benighted space station to investigate some suspicious signals, you'll soon embark on a broader quest that sees you travel to other parts of 40k's grim, dark galaxy.

In a manner very familiar to anyone who's played more than ten minutes of Diablo or Path of Exile, you'll gather up shiploads of weapons, gear, upgrades, and consumables from your enemies' mortal remains, upgrading your loadout by equipping the cream of the crop, and recycling all the rest.

There's more than enough abilities to unlock and try out, arranged in three different class trees (shooty, stabby, or psyker) to encourage multiple playthroughs and different character builds. While there are similar content seasons to Path of Exile or Diablo IV, and plenty of extra build options thanks to DLC, this game isn't a standout in its genre - but it gets the basics right, and has some fun ideas.

A lot of thought has gone into making ranged combat genuinely interesting in an ARPG, and a dedicated cover system, and mechanics for suppression fire, do a lot to distinguish it from its peers. While it's always true that multiplayer games are better with friends, that's especially true here, because a party with mixed abilities will let you enjoy your specialization to the fullest.

If you're a 40k fan who fancies some Diablo-like action, or a Path of Exile grinder who's on a bit of a 40k kick at the moment, this is definitely worth a look. It's regularly on sale, so we don't advise buying it for label price.

Mechanicus 2 (2026)

Mechanicus 2 is the long-anticipated sequel to the XCOM-like strategy game Mechanicus. Released in May 2026, we haven't tested it yet - preparations for Warhammer 40k 11th edition kept all our writers rather busy in spring of 2026. We came away from our preview session eager to get stuck in, but it launched with very little fanfare, and has a mediocre user score on Metacritic.

Mechanicus 2 expands on the original's formula with a hugely expanded scope. The Necrons join the Adeptus Mechanicus as a playable faction with their own campaign and distinctive progression mechanics. The cast of memorable characters from the first game take on a larger role, joining your forces in battle and changing how your force fights. They even get fully voiced dialogue this time - though there's an option to return to Lingua Technis technobabble if you prefer.

Upcoming Warhammer 40k videogames to watch

Honestly, 2025 was rather quiet year for 40k videogame releases. The only prominent new licenced titles were, er, not new - they were remasters of the original Dawn of War and Space Marine games. Both were competent and welcome, in our view, but neither offered anything fresh to savor.

Looking ahead to the rest of 2026 and beyond, though, we have a TON to look forward to. Here are the big names to keep in mind and trailers to watch…

Total War: Warhammer 40k

Release window: To be announced

If you thought we were in a golden age of 40k videogames before, you ain't seen nothing yet. After three blockbusting Total War titles in the Warhammer Fantasy world, and nearly ten years of constant fan debate as to whether Creative Assembly could ever pull off the same feat with GW's grimdark far future, the carnodon is finally out of the bag. Total War: Warhammer 40k is real, it's in development, and it's looking pretty damn superb so far.

There's no confirmed release window yet, and we'd suspect it's still a ways off. But, encouragingly, Creative Assembly is already far enough along that its Announce Trailer, released on December 12, 2025, features actual gameplay.

And oh, what gameplay it is. We see dozens of units clashing across a multi-laned ruined hive city map; close ups of Space Marine drop pods smashing down amid orky melees; huge buildings collapsing under fire; and an orbital lance strike nearly evaporating a Stompa. Then, the camera zooms out to give us a coquettish hint at the widening scale of campaign gameplay: first the orbital sphere, then the whole star system.

Across various interviews, as well as CA's Developer Roundtable video released a few days after the initial trailer, we've learned a fair bit about the game's fundamentals. Total War: Warhammer 40k will launch with four playable factions - Space Marines, Astra Militarum, Orks, and Aeldari - but CA intends to add in every tabletop army post release (no word on Zoats or Hrud yet, but give it time).

Planets have multiple cities and sites to conquer, which figure as different types of ground battles. While the exact scale of the campaign isn't entirely clear yet, CA's Steam page for the game describes it as a "galactic sandbox", so it seems likely we'll be fighting over not just planets or systems but, at the very least a whole region of space, perhaps a subsector or two.

There's a huge focus on customization, with both the trailer and other dev appearances highlighting the work CA's doing to let you paint your Astartes chapter, Waaagh!, Regimentum, or Warhost in your choice of colors.

The one area we're still really curious about is how (or even if) voidship battles are going to make it into the game. CA has shown off Imperial ships in the trailer footage, and beautiful concept art for Aeldari and Ork vessels too - but there's no detail yet on whether we'll have real time space naval battles to play, or if that aspect of 41st millennium warfare is taking place off screen for now.

Either way, there's a vast amount still to learn about this title - but it's almost certain to be one of the most momentous Warhammer 40k videogame releases of all time. You better believe we'll be watching this one like a Psyber-Eagle.

Check out Total War: Warhammer 40k on Steam.

Dawn of War 4

Release date: December 3.

It's coming. It's finally coming. Announced at Gamescom 2025 in August, Dawn of War 4 is being developed by Iron Harvest studio King Art Games, and we've seen more than enough of the game since then to be extremely excited about what we're going to get.

The initial announcement trailer hits hard.  The CGI cinematics, made by Polish studio Platige Image, feature nostalgic callbacks to the iconic DOW1 intro cutscene (screaming Orks and a tattered Blood Ravens banner) but also a cavalcade of the new, from ravaging Necrons to - trigger warning - the sudden death of recurring series character Cyrus. To learn more about how it was made, read our insider interview with Platige Image.

Right from that first trailer, Dawn of War 4 confidently showed gameplay footage to leave us in no doubt that this game is aiming to be a successor of DOW1, not the more RPG-ish sequel or the deeply unpopular third one. It's a big-armies RTS with base building, y'all!

We also know DOW4 will launch with four full factions: Space Marines (including Dark Angels specific units), Orks, Necrons, and Adeptus Mechanicus.

Since early 2026 King Art has been dropping more detailed gameplay trailers focusing on each faction. The short but sweet Dark Angels reveal above gives us in-engine glimpses of a few iconic Calibanite units, including Deathwing Terminators and Ravenwing bike squadrons, as well as modern, Primaris era Space Marine units including Repulsor main battle tanks. Oh, and their playable primarch Lion El'Jonson, of course - for about five milliseconds.

January 2026's four minute long Orks Faction Trailer goes into more granular (Waaaghnular?) detail, showcasing a bunch of classic Ork units fans would always have expected and deserved in DOW4. Accompanied by a very fancy British voiceover, we see huge blobs of Boyz and Stormboyz doing their thing, and a closer look at the game's Squighog Riders - a relatively new unit for Warhammer 40k whose models only came out in 2021.

Shootas, Flash Gitz, Deff Dreads, Battlewagons, Gorkanauts, we get a short look at them all firing their guns and punching things. We also learn that there are two force leader options in the Ork kampaign: the Bad Moonz' Gorgutz 'Ead 'Unter (first seen in DOW1's Winter Assault DLC) or Snakebite newcomer Guzcutta, a Beastboss who'll likely work best with the Beast Snagga style units (fast moving melee and squigs aplenty).

In May, the Adeptus Mechanicus Faction Trailer revealed the servants of Mars to the world. The Mechanicus are predominately a ranged force, with long ranged Skitarii Rangers and radioactive Skitarii Vanguard dashing between the legs of nimble Ironstrider Balistarii and lumbering Kastelan Robots. The biggest and most revered weapon in their arsenal is the Knight Castellan, a walking avatar of the Machine God's wrath - an ornate mech suit absolutely bristling with guns.

Leading the Mechanicus are two commanders, Techno-archaeologist Potentia Delta 9, or the Skitarii Marshall Sek-Ix-23. Potentia is more technical, able to despatch servo skulls to scout the landscape ahead and with varied upgrade paths, while Sek-Ix can buff nearby units - and can even be attached to his own infantry squad.

At the Warhammer Skulls preview in May 2026, as well as telling us when the game would release (a date that was missed to give the game more polish), King Art Games announced that it was bringing back the beloved Crusade mode from the original Dawn of War's Dark Crusade expansion - a globe-trotting campaign of conquest with persistent forces. Check out our interview with the studio's Creative Director Jan Theysen to learn more.

Barely a week ahead of the December 3 release date, a new DoW 4 trailer dropped, advertising the Commander Edition. While this mostly restated information that was already public, it did have a juicy hint about the new playable faction coming in the Aftermath DLC: the Chaos Space Marines are coming, led by Vashtorr the Arkifane!

Dark Heresy

Release date: January 28, 2027

Owlcat's Rogue Trader CRPG was a landmark, the first ever 40k CRPG, and the follow up is going to excite OG 40k roleplayers even more: it's an adaptation of Dark Heresy, the original Warhammer 40k tabletop RPG!

In Warhammer 40k: Dark Heresy, you take the role of an acolyte in the service of an all-powerful Inquisitor, tasked with rooting out heresy, corruption, and the insidious plots of aliens, mutants, and heretical cults. Warhammer 40k games FAQ

Games Workshop has been making (or at least licensing other people to make) Warhammer 40,000 videogames since 1992, when George Bush Senior was US President and cellphones were like small bricks. Consequently, there's a lot of gaming trivia for Warhammer fans to dig into - here are a few fun facts to go with our top picks above.

What was the first Warhammer 40k videogame?

The first official Warhammer 40k videogame was Space Crusade, released by Gremlin Interactive in 1992. It's a direct digital adaptation of Games Workshop and Milton Bradley's classic 1990 Warhammer board game of the same name, which sees several Space Marine squads explore a spaceship, battling Genestealers, Orks, and Chaos Marines controlled by a single game master player.

It's now available to download and play free as abandonware, too - so give it a try if you want (but beware, it can be absolutely lethal for the Space Marine players).

What's the most popular Warhammer 40k game?

We'd say the original Dawn of War is the most popular Warhammer 40k game of all time - in terms of lasting popularity, fan loyalty, and impact on the gaming community.

When it was released in 2004, it introduced huge numbers of PC gamers to the Warhammer 40,000 universe for the first time, and is still revered today as a landmark real-time strategy title that hordes of 40k fans remember fondly - even though its sequels decreased in popularity.

However, Space Marine 2 reached a truly enormous audience, and has the potential to introduce even more people to 40k. Give it time, and we're confident it will overtake its big brother.

How many Warhammer 40k games are there?

A total of 57 officially licensed, full Warhammer 40k games have been released on PC and/or console since 1992. You can find a full list of them above.

That's not counting mobile-only games like Tacticus, or standalone DLC expansions like Dawn of War 1's Soulstorm and Winter Assault.

Including mobile games and standalone expansions, the total goes up to over 70.

What's the best Warhammer 40k mobile game?

The best Warhammer 40k mobile game right now is Warhammer 40,000: Tacticus. We don't include it in our main list, which focuses on PC and console games - but if you're after a slick, playable arena battling game you can play on your phone, Tacticus is worth a go.

Tacticus' basic schtick is roughly equivalent to Plarium's mega-hit Raid: Shadow Legends; you collect characters via gacha mechanics, then form them into teams to fight turn-based grid battles in a variety of modes.

What's the best Warhammer 40k card game?

If the arena battler genre isn't your bag, and you prefer trading card games to gacha hero fights, there are a handful of different free-to-play Warhammer 40,000 digital card games across mobile and PC.

On the whole, we think the best Warhammer 40k card game is Warpforge - the most recent 40k digital card game, which emerged from Early Access in October 2024. There's a wide variety of different faction decks on offer; the gameplay is sophisticated enough to allow many of the classic TCG archetypes you may recognize from Magic: The Gathering and others; and the slick graphics on both PC and mobile deliver a nice, authentic grimdark atmosphere.

If you prefer the Horus Heresy setting, its predecessor from the same developer, Horus Heresy: Legions, is also a good shout.

Their cousin, Warhammer 40k: Combat Cards, offers a slightly different, less traditional TCG style of play, with three lanes of combat and a rock, paper, scissors dynamic for ranged, melee, and psyker characters. Cards also feature proper photos of GW 'Eavy Metal painted minis, rather than original artworks - which could be a plus or a minus depending on your taste.

That's it for our compendium of Warhammer 40,000 videogames - for now. If you've got a favorite or hidden gem to champion from that list (or just want to chat about all things grimdark) come join the Warhammer 40k discussion in our Discord community!

title: The Paint Review: Squidmar Color
content:
By now, we’re all familiar with prominent miniature artists having their own signature sets, but Squidmar takes things to another level entirely with a full range of paints bearing their name, in collaboration with Acrylicos Vallejo. I know what you’re thinking: Is this just a collection of already-existing Vallejo paints, bundled into a set with a new label? According to Squidmar themselves, the colours are all brand new formulations, rather than rebadged Game Color paints. Happily, since I already have all the Game Color paints, I can test the validity of that assertion.

It’s always a huge risk to launch a new paint line; the path of success is littered with the bodies of paint lines that burst onto the scene, launched ambitious Kickstarters and failed; or those that made big promises, failed to deliver, and faded into obscurity. Partnering with an experienced industry staple like Vallejo is a very astute move, allowing Squidmar to sidestep the headache of dealing with a paint manufacturer that isn’t already well-versed in the miniatures world.

Thank you to Squidmar and Acrylicos Vallejo for providing a sample copy of the Mega Set for review.

The entire range comprises 72 bottles: 48 regular acrylic paints, 7 metallics (not on the swatch card), 5 fluorescent paints, and 12 inks.

A quick glance at the swatches shows this to be a pretty feature-complete paint set, rather than an expansion set or otherwise - pretty much everything you need to paint the kind of colourful dark fantasy on display in the box art is here. The palette is broad and features plenty of saturated spectral colours - anyone who knows me knows that I cannot resist a good turquoise and blue palette, and Deep Blue Sea, Ghastly Turquoise, and Ocean Eyes are wonderful, especially when combined with Ghostly Ink.

The teal trio of Corrupted Emerald, Gemstone, and Spearmint also have a lot to recommend them - although they’re quite similar to the Scurvy Green BSL quartet from the main Game Color line, I actually prefer these, since they’re a little further over to the blue end of the scale than the green. If there’s one area in which the colour selection is somewhat lacking, it’s probably the greens, with two olive-y browny- greens, two straightforward warmish greens, and one cold green - since green is such a complex colour, it would have been nice to include a few more, but it’s understandable in that the regular Game Color line already has most of those bases well covered.

The skin tones also have some pretty nice options amid them as well; I don’t know what a Dunskar (presumably some kind of dwarf) is, but Dunskar Skin is a lovely, luminous pink flesh tone, while Northern Tan makes for a great, pale highlight colour - when combined with Warm Grey from the main Game Color line, it’d make an excellent Drukhari skin tone recipe.  Steve Flesh makes a good all-rounder base for skin, while Sun Kissed Skin occupies the warm and punchy Sunny Skin Tone vibe with which we’re all familiar.

Other standouts in the spectral colours include: Tulip Fever – an exceptionally punchy and bright light violet colour, and Tentacle Pink - an Emperor’s Children-esque bold pink with lots of saturation and smoothness.

Thirteen of the acrylics are either brown or grey, with some great standouts: Snow Storm functions great as a white ice-blue pastel, ideal for mixing cold highlights or just painting a cold white highlight. Ancient Tome works very well as a drab brown for basecoating and shading old, musty parchment and bone. Blackwood does exactly what it says on the tin, providing a nice shadowy forest wooden tone.

Excitingly, alongside the Game Color base of the ordinary colours, the metallic included in the range boast of possessing the same technology as the much-lauded Vallejo True Metallic Metal paints. Metallic Metal is a stupid name, granted, but it functions very nicely as a quasi-Leadbelcher and goes on very smoothly, the perfect base for any steely/irony metal.

Godly Steel is exceptionally bright and shiny, sitting in the Stormhost Silver area of the graph, but suffers a little from being splotchy and watery if you’re not very careful. Ungodly Copper, meanwhile, is a very fitting option for your Decayed Metal style dark bronzes and coppers, fitting very well alongside the muted brown tones of some of my favourite dark bronzes. That said, the metallics aren’t massively different from pre-existing True Metallic Metals - this was somewhat inevitable, since the parent range is already so expansive. This probably won’t be a problem to anyone, but it’s worth noting anyway.

The inks are excellent; the colours available add a ton of punch with their high saturation and move across surfaces easily with great flow characteristics - since they’re fully transparent, I’ve made use of them as airbrush filters and glazes and, although I’m not overly fond of the kind of glossiness you have to expect from an ink, they perform very nicely. It’s important to emphasise how saturated they are, though; if you’re not careful with your dilution, they can easily overwhelm an underpainting and squash all the contrast out of it. Deep Sea Ink is a particular standout for me; I’m an absolute sucker for an oceanic blue with the right amount of green; I used it to airbrush volumetric shadows on my Valayan Gholems. Ghostly Ink is similar, but sits in a brighter turquoise mode; I love them both, and they’ll absolutely become a mainstay of my painting.

Airbrushed shadows with Squidmar Deep Sea Ink

Fluos are always a bit of a crapshoot in my experience; some manufacturers just “get” them and some really don’t, and while these aren't the best fluos I've ever used, they do the job just fine. When I was painting High Kyng Valankrom and his war throne, I used the yellow, turquoise, orange, and green Squidmar Fluorescents to paint the glow on the respective god-face statues - by and large, they pack a good amount of punch. The turquoise is the only one that's lacking, and that's largely a result of physics. All blue fluorescent paints struggle to glow as a function of the part of the spectrum they reflect, so I can't hold the relatively weak performance of Fluorescent Ghost against it too much.

The mega set also contains five miniatures from the Squidmar fictional universe of Sona; these are scaled-down soft-plastic versions of the large-scale resin display pieces they made some years ago. I’ve seen a bit of buzz online about these lacking sharpness and detail - I think this might be the result of people seeing photos of the large-scale miniatures and being confused, certainly the miniatures in my box are detailed enough, it’s more akin to Reaper Bones than GW plastic but it’s fine for all that. The characters are well defined and make a great platform for trying out the paints. I doubt anyone is buying this set just for the miniatures, but they are nice to have anyway.

So the answer to the big question about this collaboration: Are Squidmar paints just the same as existing Game Color paints with the labels swapped? The answer to that one is easy: No, they aren't already existing Game Color paints - while there are some very close cousins among the selection, nothing is “the same” as an existing Game Color paint. It would perhaps be more reasonable and accurate to consider them more of a parallel extension of Game Color with a specific theme (somewhat dark, comic fantasy style), and a very significant one at that; with 48 new regular acrylics, the Squidmar range increases the existing Game Color palette by over 50% when taken together.

I am already an enormous fan (and frequent user) of the newly reformulated Game Color paints, and although some of the earlier ones had issues with bubbling, I’m happy to report that the Squidmar paints don’t suffer from the same foaming-up in the recesses - if you give your miniature a tap on your desk or pop the bubbles with your brush, you shouldn’t have too many problems. The formula thins down very nicely for glazing and airbrushing with a little medium, and yields a nice, smooth finish and soft colour transitions.

I tested some Squidmar Colors on this little fellow, he's unfinished but you can see that the saturation is strong

I am already an enormous fan of the newly reformulated Game Color paints, and although some of the earlier ones had issues with bubbling, I’m happy to report that the Squidmar paints don’t suffer from the same foaming-up in the recesses - if you give your miniature a tap on your desk or pop the bubbles with your brush, you shouldn’t have too many problems. The formula thins down very nicely for glazing and airbrushing with a little medium, and yields a nice, smooth finish and soft colour transitions.

The Squidmar series doesn’t have any triad or BSL system associated with it, which is slightly lacking compared to the regular Game Color series and might make things somewhat harder for beginners, since so much of miniature painting education is built around the use of a more systematic approach. It also contains a selection of inks instead of washes, which I’m absolutely fine with, but might frustrate beginner painters if they try to use them in the same way.

The Squidmar Mega Set retails for around 300 euros, which, for 72 paints and five miniatures (including one big one), isn’t bad. The Squidmar paints are straightforwardly more expensive than the regular Game Color paints (each bottle costs about 80 cents more than ordinary Game Color), but they still come in well under the cost of price-leading, smaller-bottle brands like Warhammer (and are less than half the price of Tone Pro) and Two Thin Coats.

In addition to the Mega Set, Vallejo offers an “Essentials” set, which, as you might expect, is a stripped-down version of the main offering. The essentials set excises all of the inks and fluos, 2 of the metallics, and 23 of the regular acrylics, leaving a selection of 30 paints, plus four of the miniatures (the Essentials set doesn’t include the big owl), with an RRP of 163 euros - this price is essentially the same as the BSL Color set, but with four miniatures instead of 18 paints. In addition, some (but not all) of the Squidmar paints are available in quartets, similar to how they sell TMM and Game Color paints - at the time of writing, these sets consist of: NMM Gold, NMM Steel, Leather, Demon Skin, Orc Skin, Fairy Skin, Elf Skin, and Dark Skin, retailing for 16 euros each, about 4 euros per set more than regular Game Color, which is consistent with the price of the individual bottles compared to Game Color.

In terms of cost, if you were to buy all 72 of the Squidmar Color paints individually, it’d come to the same price as the Mega Set, so the set-related savings all hinge on the value you place on the five miniatures and a free brush, which certainly will vary from person to person - to me, the miniatures are a nice little extra. Would I buy them on their own? With the exception of the owl, probably not. The main event is obviously the paints, and those are above reproach. I love Game Color already, and the Squidmar paints offer the same high-quality, deep, rich saturation, and ease of use as their Game Color cousins - the Squidmar Colors are absolutely worth your money, even at the slightly increased price.

Pros:

  • Deeply saturated colours
  • Diverse and feature-complete palette that can also be an extension to regular Game Color
  • Same excellent Game Color formula

Cons:

  • Slightly increased price over ordinary Game Color
  • Metallics not massively different from already-existing TMMs.
  • No triad system or washes.

title: Conquest: City States Terataur Prime Model Review
content:
Hello friends, welcome back to the farmyard. Farmer DanDaBossMan here to give you a “taur” of our newest edition to the barn: The Terataur Prime. This beauty can run 60mph and put a world of hurt onto anyone who gets in the way. Boy, that's a lot of beef metal.

In today’s guide I would like to introduce to you the Terataur Prime and my experiences putting it together and painting it. City States are due an update very soon so a rules review will follow sometime soon.

As always if you want to get 10% off and support Tabletop Battles you can make your Conquest purchase by clicking here. You’ll also need to enter code “TTB” at checkout.

Building the Terataur Prime

To start with the model seems to be cast resin, giving it a lot more durability and the pieces are quite chunky. (Press F to anyone who’s tried assembly flimsy plastic Inquisitors). The main body comes in one piece and you get the choice of a flaming mace or an axe as a weapon, and a choice of two heads. Because I’m a glutton for punishment I went for the flaming mace. The resin is quite crisp with strong detail throughout making it a very nice model to paint.

Terataur Prime unassembled. Credit: DanDaBossMan

The only part of the building process that was difficult was the back pipes. Make sure you hold onto them while the glue dries as I found the contact points quite shallow and kept falling off while waiting to dry.

Overall, after being filed, having a soapy bath and a brush down, building the Terataur Prime was easy so I’d probably score it as 3/10 difficulty in the worst case.

Painting the Terataur Prime

Terataur Prime (front). Credit: DanDaBossMan

Before talking through the process and scheme, these are the paints (and any Games Workshop alternatives) used for those interested:

  • Base brass: Two Thin Coats: Battle Axe Brass (Games Workshop: Warplock Bronze/Runelord Brass)
  • Base silver: Games Workshop Leadbelcher
  • Highlight silver: Vallejo Model Color Silver (Games Workshop: Runefang Steel)
  • Base yellow: Warpaints Fanatic Fiendish Yellow (Games Workshop: Averland Sunset)
  • Highlight yellow: Games Workshop Flash Gitz Yellow
  • Base pink: Games Workshop Pink Horror
  • Highlight pink: Games Workshop Emperor’s Children
  • Base green: Mixed recipe (Games Workshop Caliban Green)
  • Highlight green: Games Workshop Warpstone Glow, Games Workshop Moot Green
  • Base brown: Games Workshop Mournfang Brown
  • Base black: Warpaints Fanatic Matt Black (Games Workshop Abaddon Black)
  • Base white: Game color White (Games Workshop Corax White)
  • Base red: Games Workshop Mephiston Red
  • Black wash: Games Workshop Nuln Oil
  • Brown wash: Warpaints Fanatic Soft Tone (Games Workshop Agrax Earthshade)
  • Red wash: Warpaints Fanatic Red Tone (Games Workshop Carroburg Crimson)

As you may be able to see, I’ve been migrating away from Games Workshop paints in the last few years towards dropper bottles. Most of my paints are on their last legs from drying out due to crusting on the lid.

Terataur Prime (back). Credit: DanDaBossMan

At its most basic level the Terataur Prime is simple to paint. There are large open, flat panels and body parts and it is made even easier painting bronze and silver as these colours are quite forgiving and easy to fix.

I started by base coating the whole model brass and silver with two thin coats (thanks Duncan) before applying a liberal black wash. Once dried I highlighted the brass by using a 50:50 mix of Battle Axe Brass and Silver, followed by Silver to edge highlight and apply to the most raised surfaces to give it a super shiny effect. For the silver itself, after the wash, I highlighted with Silver all edges and raised surfaces as per the brass to make it shiny. I like it shiny.

Next up was the cloth and pauldrons. Shockingly your mileage varies here as you may want to follow the box art and do brass, bronze or gold for the pauldrons. If for some reason you want to join the Battenberg Squashies I can reveal to you my forbidden secrets of getting yellow to stay yellow.

Firstly, make sure it's primed white, such as using Games Workshop White Scar spraypaint, otherwise you’re going to have a bad time. Second, apply a base coat of Games Workshop Averland Sunset or Warpaints Fanatic Fiendish Yellow, or equivalent. You will need two, maybe three thin coats here. Next a wash of Warpaints Fanatic Soft Tone, or equivalent, watered down 50:50 and applied to the recesses. Once dried, the hard part is getting a strong bright yellow. I used Games Workshop Flash Gitz Yellow (or equivalent) and watered it down 50:50. The watering down is the important part here. When applied raw, or near raw, the paint leaves thick paint stroke marks that are hard to get rid of, and leaves visible dark streaks underneath of the undercoat. You want a strong solid layer here so apply the watered down yellow and let it pool to a reasonable degree. Once dried, apply as many coats as necessary to get the solid colour. The more the merrier. It shouldn't take many before you get a solid coat. Once done, I used Game Color White as a 50:50 mix with the Flash Gitz Yellow to start edge highlighting before finally using the White as a tip highlight on rivets and any sharp corners etc. I would say this is a delicate process and to be fair it is, getting other paints on your yellow can be an absolute pain to fix. That said I’ve found using the watered down Flash Gitz Yellow is able to cover up mistakes quite easily.

Terataur Prime (left). Credit: DanDaBossMan

As for the pink, I started with a base coat of Games Workshop Pink Horror before washing with Warpaints Fanatic Red Tone as per yellow above. Next I highlighted with Games Workshop Emperor’s Children. Thankfully this paint is strong enough to not need to be watered down like Flash Gitz Yellow so multiple applications are smooth and strong. Finally I highlighted as per yellow by using a 50:50 mix of Emperor’s Children and White.

The laurels, while blue in the box art, I decided to paint brown as leather. I used Games Workshop Mournfang Brown, washed with Nuln Oil, and highlighted back with Mournfang Brown and a 50:50 mix of White.

Next was the flaming mace. Just looking at the box art made me sweat and anxious. I decided not to use standard flame colours cuz reasons. That said, it follows the same pattern so choose any fire colour you like. This required a little bit of experimentation to figure out how best to do it.

For the grill, I started by using Games Workshop Warpstone Glow over a White basecoat. Once dried, I applied a dab of White into the ends of each side of the grill. Using a little bit of the Warpstone Glow I wet blended them together before applying a final dot of White into the corner of each recess. I then used a 50:50 mix of Games Workshop Warpstone Glow and Warpaints Fanatic Matt Black (or Games Workshop Caliban Green if you’re feeling spicey) to edge highlight the top of the grill going almost all the way to each end. Finally I used Matt Black to highlight the middle third.

Terataur Prime (mace). Credit: DanDaBossMan

I hate doing fire, even though I play Tzeentch Daemons and took it upon myself to have rainbow fire. That said, it wasn't too difficult. Start by applying a 50:50 mix of Warpstone Glow and Matt Black, or Caliban Green, from the tip of the flame to about one third from the mace. Then apply Warpstone glow to the remaining third. A liberal black wash here on the tip of the flame to the middle helps darken it down a bit. Now, this is where fire diverges from conventional painting. The inner parts of the fire are the highlights and the outer parts are darkest. So I started applying a layer of Games Workshop Moot Green to the recesses of the fire, followed by a small stroke of White. Finally I glazed with a watered down Moot Green to blend it a bit. You may notice there are reflections of the fire on the mace. This was also anxiety inducing. While not perfect I used the same glaze to highlight areas near to the flame where some green would be reflected. Not my best work but it’ll do.

The hot back pipes were another anxiety inducing affair so let me help you out here. I base coated the bottom third with Fiendish Yellow into a solid colour. After this I began mixing Games Workshop Mephiston Red with the yellow in various stages, a tiny bit of red at a time. This technique relies heavily on 50:50 washes like the yellow pauldrons previously discussed. With an orangey colour, I began applying watered down paint to the middle of the pipe, followed by watered down yellow below it and blending them carefully. I then applied some Mephiston Red above the orange and wet blended that before applying some Matt Black above the red and finally blended the red and black. This took several attempts as hubris got in the way and I started blending bits before they were properly dry causing me to have to go over it again. For your own sanity, wait for the layer to dry before doing another pass. You’ll find that it probably isn’t perfect but it doesn’t need to be. Don’t get cocky here like I did.

Terataur Prime (back pipes). Credit: DanDaBossMan

The black pipes were base coated with Matt Black, followed by a 75:25 mix of Matt Black and White on areas that catch the light i.e. the top. I then edge highlighted with a 50:50 mix, followed by a 25:75 mix then a watered down Nuln Oil wash to bring it all together and darken the colours a little.

For the eyes, I base coated Fiendish Yellow and began applying watered down 50:50 coats of Fiendish Yellow and Mephiston Red to get an orange and dabbing the colour carefully with a very pointy brush around the eyes. Finally I added two dots of White to complete the look.

And there you have it, one Terataur Prime a la Battenberg *chefs kiss*. It may not win any Golden Daemons, but it's done, and isn’t that the best a wargamer can ever hope for?

Terataur Prime (right). Credit: DanDaBossMan

Final Thoughts

Overall the Terataur Prime was a pleasant model to paint and very little drama other than the self inflicted mental anguish that would make a Cenobite blush. If you’re not feeling confident with flaming effects I’d highly recommend the axe instead and not worrying about the hot back pipes. The box art is always just a suggestion anyway. I had a lot of fun painting this little big guy and I’m sure you will too. If you have any questions about this model or any techniques, don’t hesitate to ask!

title: From the archives: How The Wild Beyond the Witchlight brought amateur dramatics to D&D
content:
This article was originally published on September 24, 2021.

There's a moment of theatrical greatness in the Dungeons and Dragons sourcebook The Wild Beyond the Witchlight. After spending hours exploring the magical carnival that opens the adventure, you're invited to its final performance of the evening. Entertainers crowd inside a tent, spectators fill the stalls, and the carnival's mysterious owners emerge from their private wagon for the first time. Everyone's gathered to crown that evening's 'Witchlight Monarch', bestowing upon one lucky individual the title for being a glowing beacon of good old fashioned fun.

Except you, of course. You're here to steal the owner's pocket watch from under his nose. Among all the excitement of the crowd and pageantry of the coronation, there's a daring heist to perform, and it could go several ways. You might ask the Displacer Beast you've befriended to make a distraction, or call upon the carnival's resident mime to nab the pocket watch as a favor for returning his voice. Maybe the attendant Bugbear might lend a hand with his fireworks display.

It's a grand set-piece that encourages you to lean into the mischievous and playful side of D&D's roleplaying. There's a plan to formulate and a job to do, but, as hard as you might try to prepare the perfect, professional heist, you can't escape the pantomime atmosphere of the whole stunt: you're stealing a watch, from a ringmaster, on stage, surrounded by a bunch of magical faeries. The Wild Beyond the Witchlight is a masterclass at bringing am-dram to D&D 5E - and I love it.

Some players are drawn to D&D for its residual wargaming elements. You might like to carefully min-max your character build, tactically analyse encounters on a gridded battlemap with painted miniatures, or pour over every sourcebook to find the perfect spell for your party. There's enjoyment to be had there, but it's not what draws me to the game.

I like to embrace the silliness of the whole thing: concoct an outlandish plan just to see how it pays off, or explore a new location in the hope there's some satisfying climax at the end. In effect, I want to embrace all the pomp, misplaced ambition, and excess of regular amateur dramatics. It just so happens to play out in a fantasy world.

That's all found in The Wild Beyond the Witchlight. Its Feywild setting, of course, does a lot of the heavy lifting, with its whimsical landscape and nonsensical characters (I can't remember the last time I came across a talking oil can or aristocratic bullywug in a D&D adventure). And its not so subtle riffs on classic children's novels and West End productions - like its Getaway Gang of runaway children, led by a charismatic boy hero, that may as well be called Peter Pan's Lost Boys - might be a little heavy-handed.

But it's the book's more fundamental and ambitious parts that really allow you to lean into its theatrics. With a pacifist design that lets you complete the entire adventure without so much as picking up your sword, it rewards you for thinking more creatively in your roleplaying. Why bother slaying the villain that stands before you when you could negotiate your way to victory, all while earning a bigger reward and access to tantalizing new side plots?

When the world around you isn't one of danger or impending doom, you're free to explore its limits. Ideas that would usually be too risky become appealing, and tenuous plans that test the limits of NPCs (and your DM's willpower) are probably worth a shot. There are still consequences for failure, but a world that is, by default, open to discussion rather than defined by fighting is exponentially more fertile ground for experimentation.

All of this, however, comes neatly together in the book's set pieces. Like the crowning of the Witchlight Monarch in its first chapter, The Wild Beyond the Witchlight is peppered with moments of constructed theatrics. They demand you to forget your dungeon-crawling days and simply embrace the stage with all the improvisational mishaps that involves.

The best of these moments is also the bluntest of them. Towards the end of the adventure, characters are forced into a literal performance in a hag's twisted theater production. You'll have to draw lines from a bag, and gradually ad-lib your way through a tragedy on-stage to earn the audience's favor.

It's got all the Shakespearean pomp you'd expect, and hands the entire party a wonderful moment to collectively tell a story without worrying about the numbers on their stat sheets, or how many spell slots they've got left.

The Wild Beyond the Witchlight understands the potential for drama in a D&D adventure. The kind that inspires the most creative actions of its players, and the most left field choices of DMs. It's not afraid to lean into silliest parts of D&D, and is one of the best 5E adventures for it.

Got your own table stories from the Feywild to share? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord. Or, if you want to prep for your next campaign, here's our guides to DnD classes and DnD races.
